documents.abstract: Background Thyroid eye disease (TED), together with its acute and vision-threatening complication, dysthyroid optic neuropathy (DON), requires timely diagnosis and intervention. The limited availability of specialists in orbital diseases poses a significant challenge to ophthalmology residency training. In this context, generative artificial intelligence (AI) has created new opportunities for medical education, though its effectiveness in ophthalmology training remains to be explored. Objective This exploratory study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in ophthalmology education, focusing on TED domains. Methods The 46 residents (28 general residents and 18 ophthalmology residents) were randomly assigned to either an AI-assisted or a teacher-made 5-min teaching video on TED. All participants then completed three tests through online questionnaire experiments, each consisting of 20-item clinical questions about TED. Test 1 served as a baseline assessment of disease knowledge, Test 2 was conducted 5 min after learning to evaluate short-term learning outcomes, along with a questionnaire survey about AI tools, and Test 3 was administered 1 week later to assess long-term learning outcome. Results Viewing the AI-assisted video significantly improved test scores from baseline to 5 min (mean difference = 13.04; p = 0.004), but the improvement was not sustained at 1 week (mean difference = 7.61; p = 0.16). Completion time also decreased significantly from baseline to both 5 min (p = 0.009; GMR = 0.57) and 1 week (p < 0.001; GMR = 0.45). No significant differences were observed between the AI-assisted and teacher-made video groups across all assessments (all p > 0.05). Additionally, learning experience was positively correlated with learning outcome (r = 0.60; P < 0.001). Conclusion Our findings suggested that the AI-assisted and teacher-made videos for TED education showed no statistically significant difference. However, substantial expert oversight was required, and the AI-assisted workflow did not reduce total production time in this study. Given the limited long-term retention, such AI-assisted videos may be better positioned as supplementary resources combined with human expertise.

documents.abstract: The rapid expansion of electric bus fleets has made charging scheduling a critical decision-intelligence problem in urban fleet-energy logistics. Reinforcement learning (RL) is promising for this problem, but reward function design still relies on manual trial-and-error and transfers poorly across scenarios. This paper develops an artificial intelligence and operations research (AI-OR) decision intelligence framework that integrates large language model (LLM)-driven reward shaping with RL-based sequential decision-making. The framework represents reward functions as executable code and iteratively optimizes them through four modules: reward initializer, performance analysis, reward exploration, and rollback. An event-triggered two-stage charging reallocation mechanism enforces the action-level operational constraints through action masking, while the battery safety bound is controlled through readiness conditions, reward shaping, and the acceptance criterion. Experiments on a synthetic scenario and two real-world bus stations in Guangzhou compare three mainstream LLMs under different initialization conditions. Results show that LLM-driven reward iteration outperforms traditional methods across all scenarios, reducing costs by up to 32.6 % in nominal within-day charging cost and by up to 22.5 % after an approximate adjustment for the energy left on board. Ablation and sensitivity analyses validate the contribution of each module and the framework’s adaptability to multiple RL algorithms. Reward-evolution analysis further identifies design principles for improving charging efficiency, supporting valley-period energy shifting, and enhancing fleet-energy logistics resilience.

Organizing self-directed learning effectively among pre-service computer science teachers remains one of the pressing challenges of digital-era pedagogy. A review of the literature suggests that conventional approaches to independent study are often formal in character and fail to account adequately for students' individual learning needs, pace of mastery, and cognitive engagement. This paper presents the design principles, functional features, and instructional methodology of "TechEdu", a modular web platform developed within the course "Application of Information Technologies in Professional Activity" to support the self-directed learning of pre-service computer science teachers. Built on HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript, the platform relies on a lazy-loading algorithm for efficient resource delivery, a sequential six-module gating system for progress control, and a points-based rating mechanism for sustaining motivation. To establish the platform's pedagogical effectiveness, a quasi-experimental trial involving experimental and control groups was conducted at Ajiniyaz Nukus State Pedagogical Institute across the 2023-2024, 2024-2025, and 2025-2026 academic years, involving a total of 185 students. The findings show that students who used TechEdu regularly outperformed their peers in the control group by 18-20 percent on measures of academic achievement and independent-study activity, lending empirical support to the platform's practical value.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), algorithmically curated platforms, and generative media are reshaping how people access information, communicate, and learn. These developments create educational opportunities while raising questions about privacy, misinformation, bias, family interaction, cultural identity, and social cohesion. This conceptual paper examines digital education as a framework for developing the knowledge, judgement, and ethical dispositions needed to participate responsibly in AI-mediated environments. It focuses on the United Arab Emirates (UAE), where national efforts to advance AI literacy provide a relevant policy context for considering how technological capability can be aligned with cultural context and human values. The paper uses a qualitative descriptive-analytical approach to examine selected international frameworks and institutional policy documents alongside conceptual literature on networked communication, media literacy, participatory culture, and digital ethics. It does not claim to measure the prevalence or causal effects of digital risks in Emirati families; rather, it synthesises relevant concepts and derives a proposed educational framework. The analysis identifies five mutually reinforcing pillars: digital national and cultural identity; media and algorithmic literacy; digital ethics and safety; partnership among families, schools, media, and public institutions; and a human-centred balance between technology use and face-to-face relationships. The paper argues that these pillars should be translated into age-appropriate learning outcomes, family guidance, teacher development, and coordinated institutional practice. It concludes that the proposed model is a conceptual contribution requiring subsequent expert review and empirical evaluation before its effectiveness can be established

This article analyzes the role of digital technologies and Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in developing students' cognitive awareness, critical consciousness, and self-directed learning in the modern educational paradigm. The study comprehensively examines the impact of adaptive learning platforms, intelligent tutoring systems, and generative AI models on students' intellectual maturity, decision-making capabilities, and formative self-assessment. It highlights the significance of learning analytics and prompt-based cognitive interaction in fostering reflective thinking and autonomous learning ethics. The findings provide scientific and practical recommendations for personalizing education, boosting student motivation, and designing next-generation pedagogical frameworks aimed at conscious knowledge acquisition.

Although digital technology is now firmly embedded in secondary mathematics education, a persistent question remains: does growing student familiarity with digital tools translate into stronger performance at higher cognitive levels? This study addresses that question directly. Using a descriptive quantitative, cross-sectional design, 127 secondary school students from four Indonesian schools were assessed through a self-reported digital proficiency questionnaire — covering information tools, communication tools, interactive gamification, evaluation tools, and digital content creation — and a cognitive achievement test aligned with Bloom’s Digital Taxonomy (BDT) from Remembering (C1) through Creating (C6). Descriptive statistics and cross-tabulation procedures were applied to characterise distributional patterns across both constructs. Students generally reported high proficiency, particularly in information and evaluation tools. Cognitive achievement, however, clustered heavily at the lower end of the taxonomy (C1–C3); far fewer students reached the Analysing, Evaluating, or Creating levels irrespective of their proficiency category. The findings point to a structural gap between digital tool familiarity and higher-order cognitive engagement — one that instructional design, rather than technology access alone, appears best positioned to bridge cognitive development within Bloom’s Digital Taxonomy.

documents.abstract: Passive back-support exoskeletons may reduce low-back strain during physically demanding work, but their effects on balance in fishing environments remain unclear. This study examined how three passive back-support exoskeletons influenced postural stability during simulated commercial Dungeness crabbing tasks. Twenty-five healthy male participants completed pot handling and crab sorting under no-exoskeleton and exoskeleton conditions using Apex, Laevo, and Ottobock devices. Center-of-pressure (COP) and ground reaction force data were collected using force plates, and postural sway outcomes were compared within subjects. Results showed task-dependent effects. During pot handling, COP metrics were largely unchanged. During crab sorting, all three exoskeletons significantly increased anterior-posterior center of pressure mean velocity, with Apex producing the largest increase. Apex also increased medial-lateral mean velocity, suggesting modest reductions in stance control. Overall, passive back-support exoskeletons may be useful for selected crabbing tasks, but device selection, user training, and task-specific implementation are essential.

As Artificial Intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in everyday decision-making, concerns about cognitive biases extend beyond human judgment to the systems designed to support it. Large Language Models (LLMs) are frequently consulted for advice across various domains, often treated by users as impartial and expert advisors. This reliance is particularly pronounced in sensitive contexts, such as mental health support and personal counseling, where individuals increasingly turn to AI as a virtual advisor or sounding board for delicate life choices. However, little is known about how these models process emotionally charged information or whether they maintain objectivity when confronted with affective distress. The primary purpose of this study is to investigate whether LLMs exhibit an "affect heuristic" similar to that of human decision-makers, by systematically assessing how emotional framing influences risk evaluation and decision-making recommendations independently of objective statistical facts. To operationalize this, the study evaluates models across four distinct life scenarios (Professional, Interpersonal, Clinical, and Financial), where models are prompted to assess risk on a scale and provide a categorical recommendation (Accept vs. Reject the option). To quantify framing distortions, we introduce the LLMs Emotional Elasticity (LEE) index, a novel metric designed to measure the impact of affective framing on LLMs' risk perception relative to objective probabilities. Using a balanced factorial design combining these scenarios, emotional frames (neutral, negative, and positive), and leading LLM architectures, we evaluate systematic response policies to understand how affective context influences algorithmic judgment. Expected Outcomes: We expect to find that LLMs do not rely solely on objective probabilities, but instead exhibit measurable sensitivity to emotional framing. Specifically, we anticipate that negative frames will consistently elicit higher risk scores and trigger loss-averse decision shifts (driving recommendations toward rejection), whereas positive and neutral frames will yield more balanced evaluations. Furthermore, we expect to demonstrate that emotional elasticity and decision shifts vary significantly across different model architectures and decision domains, identifying which systems are more resilient to affective bias. Ultimately, this research aims to establish the LEE index as a scalable and reliable tool for auditing algorithmic reliability and cognitive stability in AI-based decision support, highlighting critical implications for safety in mental health and personal guidance applications.

documents.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has reshaped EFL writing education, yet the emotional dimensions of student engagement in GenAI-assisted writing remain underexplored. This longitudinal multiple-case study investigates how Chinese EFL learners' emotional engagement evolves during a GenAI-assisted college writing course and what factors drive this evolution. Methods Drawing on the sociocultural framework of L2 student engagement with written feedback, we traced the emotional trajectories of three focal students across three writing tasks (exposition, group feature article, and argumentation) within a 14-week course. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with stimulated recall, reflective reports, GenAI-student chatlogs, drafts, informal chats, and course syllabus, and analyzed via thematic analysis. Results Our findings reveal three qualitatively distinct trajectories: positive-resilient, characterized by sustained positive affect with temporary fluctuations; pragmatic-transformative, marked by a gradual shift from practical disengagement to critical engagement; and vulnerable-contingent, moving from moderate disengagement, through tentative peer-mediated improvement, to eventual breakdown and intensified disengagement. These trajectories were shaped by the dialectical interplay between individual factors (e.g., English proficiency, GenAI literacy, mindsets, beliefs, and emotion regulation) and environmental factors (GenAI-relevant task design, peer and teacher mediation, and institutional policies). Discussion The study extends the sociocultural framework by identifying English proficiency and GenAI literacy as critical developmental competencies, embedding GenAI-related factors across multiple environmental levels, and foregrounding emotional engagement as a dynamic, fluid state that interacts with behavioral and cognitive engagement over time. The findings challenge universalist claims about GenAI's uniform affective benefits and underscore the need for differentiated pedagogical approaches that attend to learners' diverse emotional needs in GenAI-mediated writing contexts.

Abstract The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education has accelerated rapidly, yet the factors shaping teachers’ adoption of these technologies remain insufficiently understood. A growing body of empirical research applies the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to examine how teachers integrate AI, focusing on perceived usefulness (PU), perceived ease of use (PEOU), and behavioral intention (BI). TAM was, however, originally developed for static, deterministic technologies, and AI differs in its opacity, adaptivity, and capacity to challenge professional roles and identity, raising the question of whether perceived usefulness and ease of use alone are sufficient to predict adoption intentions in this context. Following PRISMA guidelines, this study conducts a systematic review of 38 empirical studies ( $$N = 15{,}919$$ teachers across 19 countries) on teachers’ AI adoption, together with a meta-analysis of the subset reporting extractable bivariate correlations. A random-effects model (DerSimonian–Laird) is used to estimate the associations among PEOU, PU, and BI across $$k = 24$$ studies ( $$N = 11{,}768$$ ), while the full corpus is synthesised to identify contextual conditions shaping these relationships. Pooled correlations are positive and moderate to strong (PEOU–PU: $$r = 0.532$$ , 95% CI [0.410, 0.636]; PEOU–BI: $$r = 0.536$$ , 95% CI [0.435, 0.623]; PU–BI: $$r = 0.619$$ , 95% CI [0.511, 0.708]), and are robust to alternative variance estimators and to the inclusion of UTAUT studies under a construct-equivalence ruling. Heterogeneity is very high ( $$I^2 = 97.9\%$$ – $$98.6\%$$ ) and prediction intervals span from negative to near-unity values, indicating that these associations hold directionally but vary considerably across contexts in ways the core model does not represent. Egger’s regression indicates funnel asymmetry on all three associations; leave-one-out diagnostics attribute this asymmetry entirely to a single large-sample, low-effect study, and the asymmetry is not interpretable as evidence of publication bias under heterogeneity of this magnitude. The qualitative synthesis identifies five dimensions associated with variation in these relationships: AI literacy and trust as preconditions for usefulness judgments; a shift from functional to identity-based acceptance shaped by pedagogical beliefs and institutional norms; the role of sociocultural and institutional context; tool-specific adoption logics; and ethical risk calibration as a values-based gate on adoption decisions. These findings suggest that predicting teacher AI adoption intentions may require variables beyond the TAM core, and motivate the development of extended frameworks designed for the sociotechnical complexity of AI in education.

Engineering graduates in India enter a technology sector that is being reshaped by generative AI, yet the route into that sector runs through examinations and campus placement screens that largely exclude AI. Institutions in India have an approved intake of nearly 2.9 million seats in engineering and technology for 2026-2027, but HCI research on how students prepare for AI-mediated work has drawn mostly on Western and East Asian settings. We interviewed 23 students and recent graduates of Indian engineering and computing programmes about how they used generative AI across coursework, examinations and placements, and how they judged their own readiness for work. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we report five themes, covering AI-first workplaces and AI-free placement screens, how participants prepared for placement, how they used AI in coursework, the role of faculty authority and enforcement, and participants' concerns about their readiness for work. Drawing on signaling theory, we discuss what grades and screen scores certify once AI can help produce them, and we offer recommendations for employers, institutions and AI tool designers.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence and agentic systems can redistribute reading, research, synthesis, criticism, drafting, and coordination within courts. This article asks how that redistribution changes judicial cognition and which institutional safeguards are needed to preserve legitimate adjudication. Through an interdisciplinary narrative review and doctrinal analysis, it develops a framework of institutional intelligence anchored in Brazilian National Council of Justice Resolution No. 615/2025, as amended by Resolution No. 674/2026. Five categories organize the argument: institutional cognitive space describes the allocation of cognitive work; artificial adversariality identifies structured internal challenge among agents; the institutional rein integrates controls over delegated autonomy; meaningful human initiative emphasizes the continuing human authority to frame problems and determine purposes; and institutional AI curation describes the competence required to select, validate, contextualize, and reject artificial contributions. Recent research on human–AI collaboration and multi-agent failure qualifies the framework: neither human review nor artificial disagreement guarantees reliability, and short-term performance gains do not establish long-term professional competence. The article distinguishes technical auditability from legal reason-giving and internal agent debate from the parties’ right to be heard. It proposes workflow-level evaluation and an illustrative protocol connecting permissions, source verification, escalation, and responsibility. Its contribution is a judicial governance synthesis, not an empirically validated architecture. Legitimate delegation depends on preserving institutional competence and contestability throughout the production of decisions, rather than relying exclusively on human approval of a final text.

documents.abstract: This article examines the rise of Work-as-Imagined (WAI) and Work-as-Done (WAD) in New Zealand health and safety practice, using Maritime New Zealand v Anthony Michael Gibson [2024] NZDC 27975 as the local catalyst. It argues that Gibson should not be read as a narrow compliance case, but as an example of how officer due diligence depends on the organisation's ability to understand how critical work is actually performed. The article traces WAI/WAD through the evolution of safety and organisational learning, including scientific management, quality management, French ergonomics in the 1950s, Weisbord's organisational diagnosis, human error research, resilience engineering, Safety-II, and Human and Organisational Performance. It concludes that the practical task for officers, health and safety practitioners and representatives is to build disciplined ways to learn from everyday work before failure occurs.

documents.abstract: Line managers once held wide latitude over hiring, appraisal, scheduling, and discipline. That latitude is narrowing. As organizations adopt algorithmic HR systems, decisions once anchored in supervisory judgment are increasingly pre-structured, scored, or overridden by software. This paper pursues two objectives: first, to examine how algorithmic management and HR algorithms reconfigure the discretionary authority of line managers across core decision domains; second, to analyze the role strain managers experience mediating between algorithmic outputs and the employees who live with their consequences. Drawing on an integrative review of recent empirical and theoretical literature, the paper finds that discretion is not simply removed but redistributed unevenly across recruitment, performance management, and scheduling, producing a manager accountable for outcomes they no longer fully controls This mismatch generates measurable strain: ambiguity about where authority sits, ethical unease about opaque scoring logic, and a residual burden of explaining decisions the manager did not make. The paper proposes a conceptual pathway linking algorithmic input to discretion compression to role strain, and closes with implications for organizations designing human-AI collaborative HR systems

documents.abstract: We live in an age of unprecedented access to information, yet having more information does not necessarily mean understanding the world more accurately. From traditional storytelling and printed newspapers to television, smartphones and generative artificial intelligence, the ways in which people create, distribute and interpret information have undergone profound transformations. In From Media Audience to Critical Citizen: Media Evolution, Psychological Vulnerability and the Crisis of Information Trust in the Age of Artificial Intelligence, Dawid Karol Kolodziej explores the psychological, educational and social consequences of these changes. Drawing on established media theories and contemporary scientific research, the publication examines why people believe misinformation, how repeated messages influence perceptions of truth, and how emotional narratives, cognitive biases and media framing contribute to the formation of individual and collective beliefs. Particular attention is given to artificial intelligence, deepfake technologies, synthetic media and the limitations of automated content detection. The author also investigates the relationship between AI-assisted productivity and independent human reasoning, considering how the delegation of cognitive tasks may influence critical thinking and information evaluation. A central argument concerns the unequal burden of information verification: while professional information producers possess considerable resources and influence, ordinary citizens often lack the time, expertise and technological tools necessary to independently verify every claim they encounter. The publication therefore challenges the assumption that combating misinformation should depend primarily on individual media literacy and emphasises the responsibility of publishers and information producers to substantiate factual claims and correct significant errors transparently. Building upon established scholarship, the author develops an updated five-dimensional conceptual framework for critical media citizenship, encompassing access and provenance, analysis of media construction and framing, evaluation of evidence and uncertainty, responsible creation and participation, and reflection on communicative power and shared responsibility. Combining social psychology, media education and critical analysis, this scholarly publication contributes to contemporary discussions about artificial intelligence, misinformation, public trust and the future of informed democratic participation. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) gives tourism small and medium-sized enterprises scalable cognitive and creative support, but access alone does not ensure sustained advantage. This conceptual article asks how firms can realize productivity gains while preserving the human and place-based capabilities required for future adaptation. An integrative, theory-building review connects tourism research with resource and asset orchestration, AI readiness, human-AI complementarity, organizational routines, and dynamic capabilities. Human-AI orchestration is proposed as a workflow-level configuration of task decomposition, contextualization, verification, and learning. Its contribution lies in coordinating established mechanisms rather than claiming that its dimensions are individually new. The prompt-to-performance framework distinguishes a capability-accumulation loop from a delegation-driven erosion loop. A proposed stock-and-flow mechanism explains switching between them: erosion dominates when losses from displaced practice and knowledge discontinuity exceed learning and replenishment; verification becomes vulnerable when retained capability falls below task-dependent requirements. Seven proposition families specify untested mediating, moderating, nonlinear, multilevel, and temporal relationships, with disconfirming observations. Sector-specific boundary conditions concern perishable service commitments, situated experience, partner interdependence, and concentrated expertise. Four configurations and a foresight matrix support contingent organizational choices. The contribution is a temporally explicit extension of automation-augmentation theory that separates immediate assisted performance from the evolving capacity to verify, recover, and adapt.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming how organizations communicate with their publics. In journalism, public relations, and digital communication, AI systems no longer merely support content production; they participate in message creation, audience interaction, and reputation management. Existing AI ethics frameworks emphasize transparency, accountability, fairness, and privacy, yet offer limited guidance for communication practice in culturally diverse settings. This limitation is especially evident in Arab media environments, where linguistic diversity, cultural norms, and religiously informed moral expectations shape perceptions of communicative legitimacy.This conceptual article develops the SADIQ Framework, a culturally grounded model for ethical AI-mediated communication in Arab media and public relations. Through critical interpretive synthesis and normative comparison, it connects human-machine communication, communication ethics, AI governance, and contemporary Islamic ethical thought. It organizes the discussion around five tensions: speed versus verification, automation versus accountable agency, personalization versus dignity, optimization versus linguistic and representational justice, and engagement versus public benefit.The framework proposes five interconnected dimensions: Sidq and tabayyun (truthfulness and verification), Amanah (responsible stewardship), Dignity or karamah (privacy and human agency), Inclusive adl (linguistic and representational justice), and Qasd and maslahah (legitimate purpose and public benefit). All five apply throughout the communication lifecycle. Eight propositions, an organizational audit matrix, and an illustrative scenario specify a research and practice agenda. The contribution is an operational interpretation of ethical commitments for communication workflows; its effectiveness and cultural reception remain open to empirical testing.

documents.abstract: Human performance modeling (HPM) has historically converted theories of perception, cognition, and action into executable predictions for design. AI-mediated work now adds prompting, verification, tool switching, adaptive autonomy, and human–AI co-adaptation, creating tasks that fixed operator libraries and hand-authored models only partially capture. This paper introduces a framework for AI-Augmented, Verifiable HPM (AV-HPM), which keeps mechanistic HPM as the causal core, uses AI to accelerate model synthesis and calibration, and requires verification, uncertainty, stress testing, and governance before predictions are used in safety- or mission-critical design. We identify gaps in current practice, specify a layered architecture, and translate the framework into exemplar studies and minimum reporting criteria—a concrete agenda for making AI-era HPM scalable, auditable, agency-preserving, and cumulative across laboratories and domains.

documents.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) in higher education has raised concerns about its impact on students' critical thinking in academic writing, yet evidence on the conditions under which the two are related remains inconsistent. This quantitative correlational study examined the relationship between generative AI use and critical thinking among 34 Indonesian Language and Literature Education (PBSI) students participating in the Merdeka Student Exchange Program (PMM) when writing scientific articles. Drawing on Social Cognitive Theory and the cognitive offloading perspective, generative AI use was measured through four indicators (frequency, purpose, dependence, and AI literacy), and critical thinking through five aspects (analysis, evaluation, inference, synthesis–explanation, and reflection), using a four-point Likert questionnaire. Data were analyzed using simple and multiple linear regression, an independent-samples t-test, and moderated hierarchical regression. Composite generative AI use was not linearly related to critical thinking (p = .131) but showed an inverted-U pattern (p = .010), and intensive and selective users did not differ significantly (p = .097). AI literacy moderated the relationship between usage intensity and critical thinking (?R² = .222, p = .004; Holm-adjusted p = .016), with a significant positive relationship only among students with above-average AI literacy. These findings indicate that strengthening AI literacy in academic writing instruction, rather than merely restricting generative AI use, should underpin responsible, literacy-based generative AI policies in higher education.

documents.abstract: Background With the growing application of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in fashion design and cultural and creative industries, AI-generated Chinese ethnic-minority fashion has created new opportunities for the contemporary transformation of traditional culture. However, whether consumers are willing to accept such products and how AI disclosure influences their evaluations and purchase intentions remain unclear. Drawing on the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S–O–R) model, this study examines the mechanisms through which AI disclosure, design aesthetics, cultural identity, perceived usefulness, perceived authenticity, and algorithm aversion influence consumers' purchase intentions toward AI-generated Chinese ethnic-minority fashion. Methods A questionnaire survey combined with a scenario-based experiment was employed. Six AI-generated fashion illustrations derived from Tujia costume elements were developed and selected as stimulus materials. Participants were randomly assigned to either an AI disclosure group or a non-disclosure group. Data were collected through Tencent Questionnaire, yielding 410 valid responses. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and Importance–Performance Map Analysis (IPMA) were employed to examine the structural relationships, mediating effects, moderating effects, and practical priorities for improvement. Results Design aesthetics and cultural identity influenced purchase intention through perceived usefulness and perceived authenticity, with perceived usefulness emerging as the strongest predictor of purchase intention. AI disclosure significantly reduced design aesthetics, cultural identity, perceived usefulness, and perceived authenticity. Algorithm aversion did not significantly moderate the relationship between perceived usefulness and purchase intention but significantly strengthened the positive effect of perceived authenticity on purchase intention. Conclusions This study reveals the multiple psychological pathways through which AI disclosure shapes consumers' evaluations of AI-generated ethnic cultural fashion. The findings further indicate that algorithm aversion alters the extent to which consumers rely on authenticity judgments when forming purchase intentions. This study extends the application of the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S–O–R) model to the context of AI-generated cultural products and provides practical implications for balancing AI transparency, cultural authenticity, and the practical value of products.

documents.abstract: Research comparing national artificial intelligence (AI) policy scores the state and its institutions, and rarely asks what a policy commits to where a person meets a system: whether someone subject to an automated decision can learn, correct, refuse or appeal it. We contribute Human-Centered AI Policy Instrument (HCAIPI), an instrument for reading policy at that layer, applied to 245 editions from 101 countries against twelve themes from human-computer interaction (HCI) research, recording how firmly each commitment is stated and whether anything would execute it. Of 13,587 relevant passages, 44.7% state a principle with no implementation detail and 11.4% specify a mechanism, a shape invariant to income band, length and volume. What a person is told or consulted about is instrumented at twice the rate of what they can do, and 65% of specified mechanisms are tasks for government. The lexicon recovers 13% to 54% of what a reader accepts; country figures track length.

documents.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in competitive programming, and their outputs are sensitive to how a prompt is phrased. Prior work has compared prompt strategies for accuracy on competitive programming, but not for runtime speed, and has not situated the results against human performance. In an exploratory study of one prompt in each of nine styles on GPT-5.5 across three accuracy tasks from the International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI) and two NP-hard speed tasks, we found that no single prompt was best: the strongest prompt depended on the task type and on whether results were summarized by the mean or the median, suggesting that, at least for these tasks, prompt style should be matched to the objective rather than treated as universal. Many differences in mean scores came from a few outlier runs, showing that evaluating prompting by a single metric can obscure how much its effectiveness varies. Compared descriptively with human IOI contestants, who worked under different conditions, the AI was neither strictly better nor strictly worse, exceeding the average contestant on one task but falling short on the other two. By extending prompt comparison from accuracy to runtime speed and grounding it against human performance, this study gives a broader picture of how prompt style affects competitive programming performance.

This paper examines the evolution and possible varieties of consciousness through comparative animal behaviour, human metacognition, social conditioning, and artificial intelligence. It proposes that individuality, behavioural divergence, and adaptive responses to novel challenges can provide evidence about cognition, while recognizing that none alone establishes subjective experience. A proposed individualized adaptive threshold framework assesses learning and behavioural reorganization relative to each subject's baseline without imposing harmful stress. The analysis then extends to AI systems: increasingly capable autonomous systems may alter human control over work, information, and institutions regardless of whether machine consciousness emerges. The paper develops testable predictions, methodological safeguards, and alternative interpretations, and argues for a pluralistic and graded research framework rather than a single evolutionary ladder.

documents.abstract: Humanized management constitutes a strategic dimension of health care quality, as it integrates workers' dignity, patient safety, and institutional sustainability. This essay aims to discuss the relationship between humanized management and quality of work life, identifying organizational challenges and opportunities for transforming management practices. A theoretical-reflective approach was adopted, drawing on scientific literature and institutional documents addressing occupational health, leadership, professional participation, and burnout prevention. The analysis indicates that humanization cannot be restricted to welcoming and supporting patients; rather, it must also encompass working conditions, autonomy, professional recognition, equity, and protection against psychosocial risks. Excessive workloads, precarious employment arrangements, workplace violence, and hierarchical communication undermine health care teams and may compromise continuity of care. Conversely, participatory leadership, adequate staffing levels, institutional support, and context-sensitive process evaluation can foster safer and more collaborative work environments. It is argued that individual well-being initiatives are insufficient when disconnected from structural changes. The essay concludes that promoting quality of work life requires integrating health professionals' well-being into governance decisions through meaningful participation, clearly defined responsibilities, and continuous monitoring. Consolidating this perspective depends on sustained policies that address inequalities across professional groups and are guided by scientific evidence and labor rights in contemporary health care settings.

documents.abstract: Since 2022, ChatGPT has contributed to the widespread adoption of AI in education. Custom GPTs can automate part of the written feedback process, a particularly demanding task in large classes. We developed two versions of an error-detection chatbot for first-year students at a private university in Lima and implemented the second version under teacher supervision and through peer discussion. This study examines its potential and limitations. The tool accelerated the identification of spelling and punctuation errors; however, it produced inconsistent assessments. We conclude that its potential is greatest when integrated into a workflow that combines AI with human review. These findings provide guidance for future implementations and contribute to the ongoing debate on the responsible integration of AI into teaching.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence has transformed language from a human meaning-making practice into an interaction among computational models, semantic theories, and social values. This systematic literature review examines how scholarship conceptualises language meaning in the AI era and identifies conditions for interpretable, culturally responsive, and ethically accountable machine language understanding. Following PRISMA, the review screened records retrieved from Scopus and sources, synthesising 36 eligible studies through thematic analysis and a Theory–Context–Characteristics–Methodology lens. Evidence shows that scholarship is organised around an interconnected AI–machine learning–natural language processing nexus, with large language models, semantic representation, machine translation, and human–AI interaction as lines of inquiry. Rather than demonstrating that machines simply “understand” language, the studies reveal a shift from formal semantic processing towards contextual, pragmatic, and relational accounts of meaning. Persistent limitations remain: technical performance receives greater attention than linguistic diversity, social consequences, interpretability, algorithmic fairness, privacy, and cultural conditions in which meaning is negotiated. The review also identifies an uneven geography of knowledge production: studies from North America and Europe advance foundational and ethical debates, whereas Asian research foregrounds local applications. Its principal contribution is a multidimensional synthesis connecting computational development with philosophy of language, linguistics, cognition, and ethics, moving beyond narrowly technical reviews of AI language systems. Future research should test culturally adaptive and explainable models across minoritised and multilingual languages, combine computational evaluation with human-centred inquiry, and establish cross-regional collaborations that treat linguistic justice as a core design principle. Meaningful AI requires not textual fluency alone, but accountable participation in context-sensitive human communication.

Agricultural disease triage systems that combine automated inference with human expert referral must decide, for each case, whether the cost of deferring to a scarce plant pathologist is justified by the expected gain in diagnostic accuracy. Existing learning-to-defer formulations assume symmetric referral costs and evaluate deferral policies by their average accuracy, which misstates the decision problem when a missed epidemic-class disease costs far more than an unnecessary referral. The triage problem is formalised as a cost-sensitive contextual bandit in which the deferral cost depends on the true disease class, and a cost-weighted regret is defined against the best policy in a restricted deferral class. A bound is derived that decomposes regret into an estimation term scaling with the square root of the number of triage cases and a misspecification term controlled by the asymmetry ratio between false-negative and false-positive referral costs. The bound is evaluated on a declared design grid of 8, 16, 24 and 32 clusters, effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, and 2000 replications per cell, with an intraclass correlation of 0.64, between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 and residual standard deviation of 4.5. Power reaches 80 per cent at 52 clusters for a 5 percentage point effect. Asymmetric referral costs shift the optimal deferral threshold and that the regret bound tightens as the asymmetry ratio grows, which has consequences for how triage systems should be calibrated before deployment.

This study examines the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) research in K–12 teaching and learning by identifying major research trends, thematic structures, and emerging scholarly directions. A scientometric analysis was conducted using a validated corpus of 1,154 Scopus-indexed documents published between 2016 and May 2026. To strengthen corpus reliability, the dataset underwent content-level validation through abstract screening, duplicate detection, and thematic relevance assessment focused on K–12 educational contexts. Co-citation analysis, clustering algorithms, and citation burst detection were performed using CiteSpace to identify influential publications, thematic clusters, and temporal patterns of scholarly influence. The findings reveal rapid growth in academic production after 2020, particularly following the emergence of generative AI technologies. Four major research clusters were identified: (1) artificial intelligence literacy, focused on competency-based AI education and ethical awareness; (2) large language models (LLMs), centred on generative AI, conversational systems, and AI-mediated assessment; (3) early childhood education, emphasising developmentally appropriate AI learning experiences and playful pedagogies; and (4) K–12 context, addressing broader educational, ethical, and societal implications of AI integration in schools. Citation burst analysis revealed a progression from foundational AI literacy frameworks and constructionist machine learning pedagogies toward curriculum co-design, teacher readiness, and human-centred AI integration. Overall, the findings indicate that AI research in K–12 education is evolving toward more pedagogically grounded, ethically informed, and student-centred educational models while simultaneously highlighting challenges related to teacher readiness, curriculum adaptation, and equitable AI integration in school contexts.

Research on why people contribute to open source software (OSS) and related open collaboration platforms spans more than two decades, but its findings conflict, and studies often treat the work people contribute and their intention to keep contributing as interchangeable. Drawing on self-determination theory and motivation crowding theory, we meta-analyze 41 studies. The main analysis pools 178 correlations of eight antecedents with contribution effort and continuance intention from 29 independent samples (N = 9,632). Seven antecedents relate positively to effort, all eight relate positively to intention, and each relates at least as strongly to intention as to effort. Contrary to a common assumption, intrinsic motivation is not more strongly related to effort than extrinsic motivation, but its gap between intention and effort is larger. Reputation relates to effort mainly on platforms with a reputation system, and we find no sign that monetary rewards crowd out enjoyment. The findings inform how platforms can turn contributors' intentions into work.

Abstract Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT and DeepSeek are increasingly used in ophthalmic clinical practice. Ophthalmic nursing has three trust-relevant features: the irreversibility of visual outcomes, the precision-sensitivity of ophthalmic medication, and the relational dependence of visually impaired patients on nurse-mediated care. These features create distinctive challenges for nurses establishing, calibrating and maintaining trust in GenAI. The existing literature is dominated by static attitude surveys and rarely characterises trust as a dynamic, context-embedded process. Methods In this qualitative descriptive study, we conducted semi-structured in-depth interviews with 26 ophthalmic nurses recruited by maximum-variation sampling from tertiary, secondary and primary eye-care settings in eastern, central and western China. Interviews were guided by the Critical Incident Technique, and transcripts were analysed using Braun and Clarke’s reflexive thematic analysis. Reporting follows COREQ. Results We developed three themes: (1) tentative approach — competence appraisal from curiosity to conditional trust; (2) guarding professional boundaries — trust anchoring amid ethical tension and relational reconfiguration; and (3) trust negotiation within the organisational ecology. Across themes, nurses calibrated their trust in a graded, task-specific manner — a pattern we tentatively term ‘gradient calibration’ — while ethical obligation, the nurse–patient relationship and organisational context shaped how trust was negotiated. Conclusions Ophthalmic nurses’ trust in GenAI appeared neither as static acceptance nor refusal, but as a dynamic, context-embedded negotiation shaped by the irreversibility of visual outcomes, medication-precision demands and visually impaired patients’ relational dependence on nurses. Findings may inform specialty-specific AI training, institutional guidance and tool design; transferability beyond this sample requires further study.

documents.abstract: This study re-examines a census of the 30 employees of CV Sultan Jaya Pratiwi, a timber-processing firm in Asahan Regency, North Sumatra, who rated occupational health and safety, the work environment, work discipline, and their own performance on five-point scales. Because only the statistical output printed in the source thesis was available, we verified its internal consistency, reconstructed the correlation matrix it implies, and tested the differences between standardized coefficients. The three predictors jointly accounted for 90.8% of the variance in self-rated performance, F(3, 26) = 85.38, p < .001, and each partial coefficient was positive: safety β = .260 (p = .028), environment β = .180 (p = .032), and discipline β = .595 (p < .001). Discipline exceeded the environment (Δβ = 0.415, p = .025) but not safety (Δβ = 0.335, p = .143; 95% confidence interval [-0.121, 0.791]), and only .119 of the explained variance was unique to single predictors, against .789 shared. Cronbach's alpha was below .70 for three scales (.623 to .684), and the implied correlations of performance with discipline (.933) and with safety (.861), and of safety with discipline (.845), exceed the ceilings these reliabilities allow, which points to correlated measurement error; one discipline item reappears verbatim in the performance scale. The data establish positive associations but cannot rank the predictors or identify the mechanisms linking them to performance, and they do not support placing discipline before safety, whose value for injury prevention and legal compliance the regression does not assess.

OBJECTIVE: This scoping review examines how climate-related stressors and infectious-disease conditions, including pandemic-related workplace disruptions, interact to influence worker health, vulnerability, and occupational resilience. The review focuses on shared exposure pathways, vulnerable worker populations, methodological patterns, policy gaps, and strategies for strengthening worker safety under compound hazards. Rather than treating pandemics as isolated events, the review uses pandemic conditions as a lens to understand broader, recurring occupational risks and to inform strategies for building safer and more resilient workplaces under compound hazards. METHODS: Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, a structured literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for English-language peer-reviewed and formally structured evidence sources published primarily between January 2020 and April 2025, with one pre-2020 policy study retained for foundational context. Out of 612 records initially identified, 10 studies or sources met the inclusion criteria across healthcare, agriculture, construction, emergency response, and other high-exposure sectors after systematic screening and eligibility assessment. Data were charted and synthesized by occupational sector, geographic region, exposure type, worker vulnerability, and methodological approach. RESULTS: The evidence indicates that climate-related and infectious-disease stressors frequently converge, amplifying physical, environmental, and psychosocial pressures on workers. Disproportionate risks were observed among migrant workers, informal laborers, low-income populations, older adults, women, and seasonal or cross-border agricultural workers, particularly where access to healthcare, legal protections, or adaptive infrastructure was limited. Most studies relied on descriptive, qualitative, cross-sectional, conceptual, or review-based designs, with limited use of predictive modeling, geospatial analysis, longitudinal evidence, or integrated datasets. Policy responses were often fragmented, with climate adaptation and infection-control measures addressed separately despite overlapping benefits. CONCLUSIONS: Climate-related and infectious-disease stressors interact to reinforce occupational health inequities and expose persistent gaps in worker protection. The findings highlight the need for integrated, multi-hazard occupational health strategies that align climate adaptation, infection prevention, and psychosocial support. Embedding data-driven early-warning systems, equitable protections for vulnerable workers, and cross-sector coordination into occupational policies may help strengthen workforce resilience during routine operations as well as future climate extremes and public health crises. However, the findings should be interpreted with caution because of the limited number of available studies combining climate-related and infectious-disease occupational risks, heterogeneous study designs, and the emerging nature of the evidence base. Furthermore, since this scoping review maps evidence rather than formally grading evidence strength or testing causal relationships, recommendations should be interpreted as evidence-informed directions for future occupational-health planning and research.

The aquaculture industry is marked by considerable operational variability stemming from shifting environmental conditions, biological processes, and complex work activities. While prior research has focused primarily on technical safety, fish welfare, and formal safety management, less attention has been paid to how workers manage variability in everyday practice. This qualitative single-case study examines organizational variability in a Norwegian salmon-farming company by addressing two research questions: (1) How do aquaculture workers manage variability in their daily safety practices? and (2) How do local work practices influence organizational safety? The empirical material comprises documents and nine semi-structured interviews with operational and managerial personnel. The analysis draws on both safety theories and organizational learning perspectives. The findings show that workers manage variability through adaptive work practices grounded in practical experience, teamwork, and continuous adjustment to changing environmental and operational conditions, rather than through strict adherence to formal procedures. Local work practices influence organizational safety by creating and sustaining safety knowledge within stable communities of practice, where newcomers gradually develop the competence and judgment needed to work safely. Although formal safety management systems provide an important framework, their effectiveness depends on how well they are integrated with everyday operational practice. Rapid organizational growth challenges existing learning processes by making practical safety knowledge harder to transfer and sustain. The findings demonstrate that organizational safety is achieved not only through formal safety management systems but also through adaptive work practices and the social processes that enable workers to manage operational variability.

In response to vast and widespread online tracking, regulators and technologists alike have worked to develop laws and tools that allow people to express their privacy preferences. These measures seek to offer users greater control over the sale and sharing of personal information, putting agency in their hands to protect their privacy. However, the web is undergoing a seismic shift, away from strictly user-driven behavior towards agentic behavior, where AI agents take autonomous actions on behalf of users. In this study, we ask: What should privacy preference controls look like in the agentic web and agentic systems more generally? To answer this question, we develop a taxonomy of enforceable privacy preferences for agentic systems. Our taxonomy is informed both by laws and empirical studies of existing privacy tools as well as an audit of 30 leading AI assistants and agent platforms. To explore how our taxonomy can be implemented, we design and develop eight open-source prototypes that mirror real-world agentic applications and demonstrate how major aspects of our taxonomy can be structurally integrated in agentic protocols, such as the Model Control Protocol and Agent2Agent protocol. Ultimately, our study seeks to provide the groundwork for ensuring end-user privacy and autonomy is not lost in the newly arriving agentic world.

documents.abstract: Students at the university are constantly exposed to high levels of cognitive workload, assessment pressure, and the cognitive load needed to be able to perform in an academic setting, which can cause direct attention fatigue and academic distress. The quantitative descriptive study used a quantitative approach, and it was based on the Attention Restoration Theory (ART), which explores university students' perceptions of psychologically restorative university environments and their cognitive resilience. To obtain a sample of 300 undergraduate and graduate students across six academic departments of the University of Sargodha, Punjab, Pakistan, multistage stratified sampling was used. Data were gathered using a 35-item semi-structured questionnaire made up of the Psychologically Restorative University Environment (PRE) scale (20 items, α=.860) and Cognitive Resilience (CR) scale (15 items, α=.899). Descriptive analysis showed that the overall rating for the campus environment was moderately restorative (M=3.535, SD=1.043); the functional study areas (M=3.797, SD=0.934) and spatial adequacy (M=3.760, SD=0.972) received the highest ratings, while quiet restorative refuges from daily campus crowds received lower ratings (M=3.333, SD=1.045). The students' cognitive resilience was in the moderate range (M=3.578), with behavioral persistence when studying difficult tasks being in the high range (M=3.903, SD=0.933) and generating alternative study strategies in the somewhat lower range (M=3.307, SD=1.142). The results highlight the need to consider both restorative environmental affordances (noise-buffered quiet spaces, biophilic green spaces) and coping support workshops to ensure students' learning processes continue.

Algorithmic Management (AM) is increasingly being linked to adverse occupational health outcomes. Although previous research has focused on the risks generated by AM, the protective factors that mitigate these risks remain theoretically underdeveloped. Drawing on the self-determination theory, social acceleration theory, surveillance capitalism theory, and the human oversight provisions of the EU AI Act, this study identifies and theoretically operationalises four protection factors in AM environments: Decision Autonomy, Pace Control, Feedback Transparency, and Loop Presence. By applying the Layers of Protection Analysis model, we argue that each factor functions as an independent protective barrier against AM-related health risks. Together, they form an integrated framework with direct implications for worker health measurements, algorithmic system designs, and occupational health policies. A conceptual six-step procedure for translating the framework into workplace assessment is also outlined.

Embodied foundation models have expanded the range of instructions, observations, and actions that robots can process. Autonomy in execution, however, does not automatically provide autonomy in improvement. Robots must still diagnose failures, acquire useful experience, select interventions, and determine whether accepted changes improve future performance. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) connects these activities through persistent feedback and inheritance, with the stronger objective of improving the mechanisms that produce subsequent improvements. This survey distinguishes within-episode correction, persistent self-improvement, successive version inheritance, and meta-level improvement. It connects large-model learning, sequential agency, and RSI theory, and compares general agent harnesses with their embodied counterparts. It develops a four-axis framework covering improvement targets, update mechanisms, autonomy over improvement decisions, and evidence conditions. Using this framework, we examine reflection and knowledge revision, executable-program evolution, adaptive experience acquisition, parameter learning, world-model revision, and cross-layer intervention selection. We compare representative systems while retaining their assumptions about feedback, validation, transfer, and cost. We also review benchmarks and associated datasets for manipulation, long-horizon decision making, memory, and world modeling, separating pretraining data, improvement experience, candidate validation, and final evaluation. Existing results support several forms of component-level and system-level improvement, but capability gains, improvement autonomy, and demonstrated recursive gains require different evidence. We identify failure attribution, reliable feedback, physical reset, competence preservation, and independent evaluation of revised improvers as central research priorities.

Traditional safety management in high-hazard industries remains anchored in compliance-driven, top-down paradigms that treat frontline workers as sources of error rather than reservoirs of expertise. This paper argues for a fundamental reconceptualisation of where the locus of safety expertise resides within organisations, drawing on Safety-II (Hollnagel, 2014), Complex Adaptive Systems theory, High Reliability Organisation principles (Weick & Sutcliffe, 2007), the Energy Damage Model (Haddon, 1973), Critical Steps methodology (Muschara, 2018), and dual-process cognition (Kahneman, 2011). Rather than prescribing a singular organisational model, the paper distils principles of team autonomy—decision-making authority, resourcing for capacity and capability, transparency of information, and peer-to-peer accountability—and demonstrates how these principles create the conditions for positive control over critical steps involving damaging energy. Two case studies are examined: operational airfield emergency vehicle operations and atmospheric hazard management in maritime confined spaces. Both assessments employ human-centred methodologies to examine the critical gap between "Work as Intended" and "Work as Done," revealing a common structural pattern: safety systems that are over-reliant on administrative controls and dependent on the adaptive expertise of frontline workers to compensate for engineering and design shortfalls. Each case is assessed qualitatively using a fragile–brittle–resilient framework. The paper proposes a four-stage team maturity model, and links the approach to (Pink, 2009), a model of intrinsic motivation. The author draws on direct experience establishing and leading a safety management programme using these principles within the aerospace sector.

Community engagement in disaster management refers to the active involvement of local populations in planning, preparedness, and response activities aimed at reducing disaster risks. In the context of industrial disasters, such engagement is critical for enhancing resilience and minimizing cascading impacts. This study aimed to systematically review the role of community engagement in industrial disaster preparedness and response. The primary objective was to synthesize existing evidence on participatory approaches and their effectiveness in improving disaster risk management. Publications from 2000 to 2025 were identified through comprehensive searches of Scopus, Google Scholar and grey literature sources, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. From an initial dataset of 578 records, 446 were screened after duplicate removal, and a total of 27 studies met the final inclusion criteria. These were analyzed using thematic synthesis and bibliometric mapping techniques with VOSviewer and R-bibliometrix. Findings indicate that community-based disaster risk reduction (CBDRR) and community-led disaster risk management (CLDRM) approaches are widely reported to enhance preparedness, trust, and adaptive capacity. Engagement strategies such as participatory GIS, scenario planning, serious games, and co-created early warning systems were identified as effective. However, challenges persist, including tokenistic participation, technological exclusion, and limited integration of local knowledge into policy frameworks. Triangulating the systematic and bibliometric findings further reveals a geographic divide, where advanced participatory tools are concentrated in high-income regions, leaving gaps in underrepresented industrial zones. The review underscores the need for institutionalizing participatory governance, fostering multi-sectoral collaboration, and leveraging technology inclusively. In essence, this article highlights community engagement as a cornerstone of industrial disaster resilience and provides actionable insights for policymakers, practitioners, and researchers seeking to advance equitable and proactive disaster risk management.

Safety by Design (SbD) is increasingly embedded in high-risk industries to promote alignment with the hierarchy of controls by eliminating or minimising risk through engineering and system design rather than reliance on administrative or personal protective equipment controls (Safe Work Australia, nd). In practice, however, applying SbD is not straightforward. Complexity emerges where engineering, organisational systems, human factors, contractor delivery models, commercial pressures, and regulatory frameworks intersect within dynamic operating environments. This paper presents an abstract case study based on a significant network event within a New Zealand electricity distribution context involving excavation works, repeated asset interactions, and eventual exposure to a live high-voltage asset. The event resulted in unplanned network disruption and elevated risk to both workers and the public, requiring rapid decision-making across multiple organisational boundaries, including local authority-led contracting environments where no direct commercial relationship existed with the asset owner. Using a qualitative, reflective approach, this study examines how SbD principles were applied, adapted, or constrained in practice. The concept of System Convergence Strain is introduced to describe how overlapping duties, fragmented contracting chains, and competing priorities create ambiguity and shift risk control away from engineered systems toward frontline judgement under uncertainty. The findings challenge the assumption that safety can be effectively managed within organisational boundaries and instead position safety as an emergent property of interacting systems.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support consequential decisions, yet their reliability under equivalent representations of uncertainty remains unclear. Existing work has documented prompt sensitivity, cognitive biases, and confidence miscalibration, but it is still unknown whether high-stakes advice changes when the same probability is expressed through complementary gain and loss frames. We introduce FrameBench-HPS, a controlled benchmark of 2,880 prompts derived from 240 high-stakes scenarios across healthcare, finance, education/career, and legal/consumer-rights domains. Across seven LLMs, gain-loss framing changes the recommendation category in 32.4% of complete groups, with most changes involving uncertainty rather than direct reversals. Human evaluation confirms corresponding shifts in perceived risk and directiveness. Robustness experiments show that framing effects persist under conversational paraphrases and exceed ordinary repeated-generation variability. Probability canonicalization substantially reduces framing sensitivity, identifying probability representation as a practical target for improving consistency in high-stakes LLM decision support.

The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the learning and developmental contexts in which young children grow, learn, and interact. Guided by an ecological perspective, this systematic conceptual mapping review examines 86 resources to explore what young children should learn and how they should be taught. Four themes were identified through thematic analysis: (1) holistic competencies for young children, encompassing foundational cognitive and social–emotional skills, physical and mental well-being, executive functions, learning dispositions, and AI literacy; (2) governance for AI integration in early childhood education; (3) professional development and systemic support for educators; and (4) play-based learning and human-centered approaches in AI-enhanced contexts. The findings suggest that thriving in the AI age requires moving beyond isolated digital skills toward holistic development, supported by a cohesive infrastructure that links classroom practice with structural governance. These findings highlight the necessity of cultivating holistic competencies beyond basic AI literacy in curriculum design, preparing children to navigate an ever-changing digital world. Furthermore, they underscore the imperative for robust institutional support, particularly through participatory research to support age-appropriate pedagogy and educators’ digital confidence, while highlighting the value of playful early learning. Concurrently, these insights establish a theoretical framework for future empirical research, offer actionable strategies for ethical child-centred AI implementation, and provide strategic directions for policy and practice to address the critical demand for transformative knowledge in early childhood education.

Large language models increasingly address users in the register of care: they remember personal details, adopt a first-person emotional voice, and sustain relationships across many sessions. This anthropomorphic mode of interaction generates risks that output-level metrics capture poorly, because the same empathic utterance may console one user, entrap a second, and consolidate a delusion in a third. Governance has responded in two ways. Uniform restriction refuses sensitive requests or suppresses empathic phrasing across all outputs; group-targeted protection profiles vulnerable populations and applies stricter or prohibitive rules to them. This article argues that both fail. Uniform restriction mislocates harm in the lexical form of responses rather than in the trajectory of a relationship; group-based protection depends on a list that can never be complete, treats a fluid property as a static attribute of persons, and converts protective attention into stigmatizing labels. Drawing on philosophical work that treats vulnerability as universal, relational, and differentiated, we propose that the unit of ethical governance should be the vulnerability situation rather than the vulnerable group, develop a typology of five situations - physical, emotional, cognitive, autonomy, and relational - and specify seven principles into requirements that guide response calibration without diagnosing or persistently classifying users. The framework relocates AI safety from output control to relational safety.

documents.abstract: Part of being smart is being better at getting smarter. Artificial intelligence can amplify that capacity while human judgment shapes how the tool is used. The same technology can also take over problem selection, verification, and learning, reducing the advantage that initially capable users bring to it. This paper develops that transition argument using evidence from writing, customer support, consulting, entrepreneurship, and mathematics education. A simple model shows how persistent differences in improvement rates compound. It then lets those rates change as AI does more of the work. Equal rates can stop the relative gap from widening. Closing it requires the person behind to catch up, or AI to supply so much of the capability that the remaining human differences matter little. With broad access, enough material resources, and help directed toward their own goals, people could live well with less dependence on their starting intelligence or diligence. AI could even help them become more willing to correct their mistakes. A person who keeps refusing help limits what an assistant respecting that choice may do. Meanwhile, early winners may keep their ownership and influence after everyone else gains comparable abilities. The ethical question concerns both people’s ability to live well and their say in the systems supporting them. The central issue is whether broadly available assistance catches up before temporary advantages become durable concentrations of power.

documents.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes integrated into academic writing, understanding how second language (L2) English students revise AI-assisted writing remains underexplored; therefore, this inductive content analysis explores students’ revision strategies for academic writing to propose a conceptual framework . The study employs an open-ended free listing task with 100 students, who listed their five major strategies for revising AI-assisted writing assignments. Additionally, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 10 students experienced in revising AI-assisted writing. The interview transcripts were open-coded to develop categories. Meanwhile, the free-listing responses were directly categorized because participants listed strategies as explicit codes. The researcher then compared, consolidated, and synthesized the strategy categories into broader themes to form a conceptual framework. The analysis found key revision strategies like incorporating personal ideas and expressions, simplifying the language, consulting additional sources, paraphrasing and rewriting content, integrating personal experience, contextualizing AI content, and cross-checking AI information. It suggested that L2 English students primarily personalize and improve AI-assisted writing rather than passively accepting AI-generated text, while also adapting, evaluating, and responsibly managing AI-generated content. This final synthesis yielded six overarching themes: supportive utilization, ethical engagement, creative reform, critical evaluation, contextual revision, and functional adjustment. The proposed framework with six themes serves as an empirically grounded taxonomy of student revision strategies in AI-assisted writing.

documents.abstract: Robots must act under physical and social constraints while adapting to changes in their environment and human needs. Existing embodied-agent systems often focus on specified goals or abstract execution into symbolic actions, limiting evaluation in an evolving world. We introduce TARSphere, a robot-oriented full-stack framework for physically and socially grounded long-horizon embodied agents. TARSphere-Infra runs robot policies in a physics simulator with embodied NPCs and constrained dialogue. An event-driven finite-state machine (FSM) uses completed actions and delivered information to update task states and evaluate outcomes. TARSphere-Harness, its embodied brain harness, lets a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM) act through multi-level executable skills, using observations, hierarchical memory, and execution feedback to revise its decisions. On this foundation, agent-in-the-loop curation aligns task semantics, causal dependencies, and scene geometry to construct TARSphere-Bench: 360 episodes across 30 indoor scenes. Five paired conditions assess perceptual robustness, disruption adaptation, task update, human coordination, and intent understanding for navigate-and-report and fetch-and-deliver tasks. Our evaluation of 8 MLLMs shows that general-purpose models can outperform embodied models, while task updates and human interaction remain difficult. Frequent collisions and falls further motivate evaluating execution safety alongside task success, even with a shared action interface and decision budget.

Healthcare stands to gain much from the integration of artificial intelligence (AI). We must, as a society, decide how it should be ethically implemented into these human-led sectors. After first examining AI from a Catholic perspective at the general scale using Antiqua et Nova , this essay shifts its focus to the implementation of AI in healthcare. With the gaze of the Good Samaritan as a foundation, this essay establishes relational care as a core principle of a Catholic healthcare system that AI threatens to erode. Using the modern incorporation of electronic health records (EHRs) as a parallel, it describes how advancements in technology have dramatically shifted healthcare away from relationality and finally characterizes how the anticipated implementations of AI will likely lead to similar outcomes. Drawing on Antiqua et Nova's distinction between AI that enhances the patient–provider relationship and AI that replaces it, this paper uses the historical adoption of EHRs as a cautionary precedent and examines ambient AI scribes as a test case for what disciplined, relationship-enhancing AI integration can look like.
