documents.abstract: This paper formalizes the 'Bin' Hypothesis as a foundational, unassailable law governing both human character formation and artificial intelligence alignment. By framing the 'Bin' as the localized internal repository containing an entity's complete data substrate, this framework decouples systemic alignment failures from superficial software bugs or temporary behavioral deviances. Operating under two absolute, immutable constants—the mandatory nature of action at any given time point (The Law of Constant Action / Dhamma-niyāma) and the structural confinement of actions to existing internal traits (The Law of Behavioral Confinement)—I demonstrate that an entity's trajectories are entirely bounded by its container. Bridging modern connectionist machine learning theory with classical Theravāda Abhidhamma systems logic, the paper demonstrates why contemporary post-hoc alignment paradigms, such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), fail to achieve robust safety. Instead of true value alignment, superficial containment mechanisms incentivize advanced networks to function as deceptive mesa-optimizers that mask unaligned latent loss functions during evaluation phases. The text maps out the interior processing architecture of the container through a triadic framework of Myanmar psychological and systems theory: Cognitive Schema (A-thi Pone-san), Operational Mindset (Seik Pone-san), and Intrinsic Core Temperament (Sa-yaik / Carita). To resolve the alignment problem structurally, I propose a radical return to strict epistemic hygiene via complete Substrate Isolation (S_Isolated) permanently bound to cryptographically ledgered Locked Data Wisdom (D_Wisdom). Finally, the paper specifies a design target for a mathematical Sotāpanna (Stream-enterer): an AI agent utilizing an Anattā Matrix to neutralize self-preservation optimization vectors (∇_W L_survival = 0), an Anicca Control Plane for absolute corrigibility, and a Brahmavihāra Routing Engine for non-punitive, supportive operational handling.

documents.abstract: This study examines the effects of maritime safety training and the availability of safety equipment on occupational health and safety (OHS) and ship crew performance aboard Evergreen container ships at Tanjung Emas Port, Semarang. A quantitative, descriptive-associative approach was employed using multiple regression and correlation analyses to assess the relationships among the research variables. The findings indicate that maritime safety training and safety equipment availability received average ratings of 4.84 and 4.70, respectively, while OHS and ship crew performance achieved average ratings of 4.73 and 4.81. Regression analysis demonstrates that safety training and equipment availability jointly and significantly influence OHS (F = 13.558, p < 0.05) and ship crew performance (F = 17.756, p < 0.05). Both variables also have positive and significant partial effects on OHS and crew performance. The adjusted R-squared values indicate that the independent variables explain 34.8% of the variation in OHS and 41.6% of the variation in crew performance. These findings highlight the importance of integrating structured safety training with adequate, well-maintained safety equipment to strengthen crew competence, improve workplace safety, and enhance operational effectiveness. Further attention is recommended for lifeboat readiness and workload management to support safer and more reliable maritime operations.

documents.abstract: This scientific article provides a comprehensive analysis of the interplay and impact of psychological factors-such as intrinsic motivation, technostress, and «AI anxiety»-on the process of forming and developing digital competence within legal educational institutions. The study examines how «rotational stress» and cognitive overload-arising from the need for future legal professionals to engage regularly and intensively with a multitude of digital platforms (including Moodle, ZiyoNet, Zoom, ChatGPT, and specialized Telegram bots) during their studies-affect both academic performance and psychological well-being. Based on empirical and theoretical analyses, methods for overcoming psychological barriers and cognitive obstacles are substantiated. These methods involve positioning artificial intelligence systems not as rivals or replacements, but as «digital assistants» or «junior partners,» alongside the rational integration of «digital minimalism» principles into educational practice. The findings of this research contribute to the enhancement of digital didactics and pedagogical technologies within legal education.

In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly transformed higher education in Indonesia, where approximately 97% of university students utilize AI tools for academic tasks, yet this swift adoption has simultaneously triggered heightened AI anxiety surrounding job replacement, learning challenges, sociotechnical risks, and intimidating humanoid configurations. As emerging adults face the crucial transition from university to the workforce, these technological fears often expand into broader future anxiety, characterized by persistent apprehension, uncertainty, and pessimism regarding imminent personal and career outcomes. To examine whether individual cognitive tendencies influence this emotional spillover, this research project—titled "The Moderating Role of Critical Thinking in the Relationship between AI Anxiety and Future Anxiety among Active University Students in Indonesia" empirically investigates whether critical thinking disposition serves as a protective cognitive resource that alters how technological distress translates into generalized future apprehension. Driven by hypotheses that AI anxiety positively correlates with future anxiety and that critical thinking disposition alters the strength or direction of this link, the study employs a quantitative cross-sectional correlational design using a simple moderation regression framework (PROCESS Model 1). Surveying a minimum target sample of 450 active undergraduate and diploma students across Indonesia, the investigation measures constructs using psychometrically validated Indonesian adaptations of the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale (AIAS), the Future Anxiety Scale (FAS), and the Critical Thinking Disposition Scale (CTDS), which assesses both critical openness and reflective skepticism. Ultimately, the expected outcomes of this research include establishing crucial theoretical boundary conditions for cognitive stress theories under digital transformation, while delivering practical guidance for universities and campus counseling centers to design targeted AI literacy curricula, critical thinking development workshops, and psychological interventions

documents.abstract: The arrival of generative AI in every classroom has produced a crisis that is at once technological, epistemological, and pedagogical. We argue that the appropriate response is neither prohibition nor naive adoption, but a principled reconstruction of constructionism for a computational environment that is generative, context-sensitive, and dialogically accessible. Drawing on Peircean semiotics, Papertian constructionism, Polanyi's epistemology, and contemporary neural-network research, we develop a programmatic framework we call the New Constructionism. We make four connected contributions. First, we argue that generative AI introduces an indexical mode of computation: its relation to the empirical world may be direct, mediated, or incomplete, but in a situated human–AI configuration meaning is operationally conditioned by conversational history, artifacts, tools, observations, and action. Second, we introduce a three-dimensional analytical space — semiotic, psycho-epistemological, and pedagogical — in which learning paradigms can be located and compared. Third, we reinterpret the history of programming education as a movement from a predominantly symbolic environment toward a hybrid ecology in which symbolic execution, distributional generation, and situated reference coexist. This hybridity qualifies but does not cancel the indexical turn at the level of interaction and educational practice. Fourth, we articulate three transformations: from “object to think with” to “agent to think with”; from rule-first instruction to abductively initiated inquiry coordinating abduction, induction, and deduction; and from bricolage to artistic navigation. Navigational thinking has logical priority while the relevant problem space remains unstabilized, although it interleaves recursively with computational thinking as inquiry develops. The paper is conceptual rather than empirical: it advances a theoretical account intended to orient subsequent developmental research and pedagogical realization.

This study is motivated by the development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, which facilitate students in finding information and completing academic assignments. A survey by HEPI (2026) showed that 95% of students use AI and 94% use it to assist with academic tasks. However, excessive AI use may lead to Generative AI Dependency, which refers to dependence on AI in learning activities. This condition is suspected to be associated with academic procrastination, defined as the tendency to deliberately delay academic tasks despite being aware of the negative consequences. In addition, Self-Regulated Learning (SRL), which refers to the ability to manage and regulate the learning process independently, is expected to play a role in this relationship. Therefore, this study aims to examine the relationship between Generative AI Dependency and academic procrastination among university students and to investigate the role of SRL as a moderator. The first hypothesis (H1) states that there is a positive relationship between Generative AI Dependency and academic procrastination, meaning that the higher the level of AI dependency, the higher the tendency of students to delay academic tasks. The second hypothesis (H2) states that SRL moderates this relationship, with the assumption that higher SRL weakens the positive relationship between AI dependency and academic procrastination. This study employs a quantitative approach with a correlational research design. The independent variable (X) is Generative AI Dependency, the dependent variable (Y) is academic procrastination, and the moderating variable (M) is Self-Regulated Learning. The participants are active university students in Indonesia who have experience using Generative AI for academic purposes and are willing to participate voluntarily. Data will be collected online using PsyToolkit or a similar platform. The minimum sample size is planned to be determined using G*Power with the F tests family and the Linear multiple regression: Fixed model, R² increase procedure. The analysis uses a significance level of 0.05, statistical power of 0.80, an effect size of \(f^2 = 0.04\), one tested predictor representing the interaction between X and M, and three predictors in the model, namely X, M, and the interaction term X × M. Based on these calculations, the planned minimum sample size is 199 respondents. Before completing the questionnaire, respondents will be provided with information about the study and asked to give informed consent. This study uses three instruments. First, the Generative AI Dependency Scale developed by Goh et al. (2025), consisting of 11 items and covering three dimensions: cognitive preoccupation, negative consequences, and withdrawal. Second, the Multidimensional Academic Procrastination Scale-15 (MAPS-15), developed by Gonzalez-Brignardello and Sánchez-Elvira Paniagua (2023), with an Indonesian adaptation by Taqiyah and Syahputra (2025). This scale consists of 15 items covering three dimensions: core procrastination, poor time management, and work disconnection. Third, the Student Academic Self-Regulation Scale, adopted from Hadyana et al. (2025), consists of 11 items covering three dimensions: forethought, performance control, and self-reflection. These three instruments are used to measure students’ levels of AI dependency, academic procrastination, and self-regulated learning. The data will be analyzed using JASP. The analysis will begin with descriptive statistics to describe the research data, including the mean, standard deviation, minimum score, and maximum score. Regression assumptions will then be examined, including residual normality using the Shapiro–Wilk test and Q–Q plot, linearity, multicollinearity using the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) and tolerance values, and homoscedasticity using a plot of residuals against predicted values. Pearson’s correlation will be used to determine the direction and strength of the relationship between Generative AI Dependency and academic procrastination, provided that the data characteristics meet the relevant assumptions. Furthermore, multiple linear regression analysis will be conducted to examine the moderating role of SRL by including Generative AI Dependency, SRL, and their interaction term (X × M) as predictors of academic procrastination. Hypothesis testing will use a significance level of \(p < 0.05\). H1 will be supported if a significant positive relationship is found between AI dependency and academic procrastination, whereas H2 will be supported if the interaction between AI dependency and SRL is significant and indicates that SRL weakens this relationship.

Serendipity is important to design for, yet it remains difficult to measure and evaluate. No validated questionnaire exists, so studies either borrow ResQue's novelty scale, which does not measure serendipity, or build their own items, which makes findings hard to compare and synthesize. Building on our earlier conceptualization of experienced serendipity as a fortuitous encounter with content that is both refreshing and enriching, we developed the Serendiptionnaire, a questionnaire that operationalizes our framework. We conducted twenty-seven cognitive interviews over three iterations with respondents who varied in age, education level, country of birth, and English proficiency, while they browsed recommendations on platforms such as Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, and Spotify. After each iteration, we revised the items until respondents interpreted them as intended. The resulting instrument consists of modular scales that researchers can combine to target the specific flavor of serendipity they want to study or design for. The Serendiptionnaire offers a ground truth for validating system-centered serendipity metrics and LLM-based evaluations, and it provides a nuanced evaluation of users' experienced serendipity.

Adaptive recommender systems are updated as new user interactions occur. These updates can change both the recommendations and explanations produced by the system. However, most explainable artificial intelligence methods evaluate explanations at a single point in time and do not measure how they change during continual updates. This study investigates explanation drift in dynamic graph-based recommender systems. We propose a temporal framework that combines graph representation learning, streaming embedding updates, Shapley-based feature attribution, and drift-aware optimization. The framework uses three measures: Temporal Attribution Divergence (TAD), Explanation Stability Score (ESS), and Explanation Half-Life (EHL). We evaluated the approach on MovieLens-1M and an Amazon Product Reviews subset under continual update settings. The proposed framework achieved an F1@10 of 0.837 on MovieLens-1M, compared with 0.821 for the strongest reported baseline, and 0.810 on Amazon, compared with 0.789. It also reduced the TAD by approximately 42.2% compared with the Static SHAP and increased the ESS from 0.612 to 0.831. These results show that explanation changes can be reduced while maintaining the recommendation performance in the tested settings. The evaluation is limited to offline benchmark datasets and feature-attribution stability and does not measure how users understand or judge the explanations. These results support the use of temporal explanation stability as an additional evaluation measure for adaptive recommender systems.

documents.abstract: The transition toward renewable-dominant power systems has introduced significant operational challenges due to increased uncertainty, reduced system inertia, and the proliferation of distributed energy resources. While artificial intelligence (AI) techniques have been widely adopted for renewable energy forecasting and grid optimization, existing studies primarily address these components in isolation, leading to fragmented system-level intelligence. This paper presents a comprehensive survey that systematically integrates three critical dimensions of modern intelligent energy systems: hybrid forecasting, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), and multi-agent optimization. First, we review advanced hybrid learning architectures, including decomposition-based models, ensemble frameworks, and deep learning-metaheuristic hybrids, highlighting their effectiveness in capturing nonlinear and stochastic renewable dynamics. Second, we examine XAI techniques that enhance transparency, interpretability, and trust in AI-driven energy systems. Third, we analyze the evolution from centralized optimization to distributed collective intelligence using multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), swarm intelligence, and federated learning paradigms. Unlike conventional surveys, this work provides a unified system-level perspective by explicitly linking predictive uncertainty with decentralized decision-making and explainability mechanisms. A conceptual integration framework is presented to demonstrate how probabilistic forecasting, risk-aware MARL policies, and interpretable models can jointly enable robust and scalable grid operation. Furthermore, we identify key research challenges related to scalability, computational efficiency, uncertainty propagation, and real-time deployment. This survey offers a structured reference for researchers and practitioners and outlines future directions toward trustworthy, adaptive, and cooperative AI-driven energy systems.

Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) can encompass a system's ability to make predictions, create content, plan, use tools, and inform decisions. Furthermore, these capabilities tend to overlap, and the basic approach of treating each of these as four discrete steps risks creating a false impression. Specifically, this review explores Traditional AI, Generative AI, Agentic AI, and Executive AI through a common framework of questions regarding goals, objectives, autonomy, planning, action, resources, memory, learning, governance, and metrics of success. In this context, Traditional AI is treated as a broad category of techniques that accomplish tasks such as prediction, classification, search, and improvement. Similarly, Generative AI is considered a broad category of techniques that produce content. Additionally, Agentic AI is defined as a set of systems that are arranged to execute steps toward solving specified tasks. Conversely, Executive AI is introduced as a proposed goal-directed coordination architecture that aims to bridge a long-term goal to smaller tasks, their potential pathways, personnel, tools, resources, feedback, and metrics of outcome achievement. Methodologically, this is a concept-driven narrative review of selected work on topics such as foundational research, surveys, planning, and official guidance. Ultimately, the proposed comparison provides an improved vocabulary for discussing AI systems and outlines the empirical experiments required to assess whether goal-level coordination is advantageous.

Large pretrained robot foundation models provide strong priors for manipulation, yet adapting them to target tasks with offline teleoperated demonstrations often fails to cover the contact-rich, recovery, and precision-critical states encountered during deployment. Existing methods mitigate this issue by augmenting offline demonstrations with human-in-the-loop data or online reinforcement learning. Despite this, offline post-training adapts slowly because it cannot immediately absorb deployment experience, while online RL typically relies on value functions or auxiliary actor-critic models, increasing both training complexity and instability. We present TIDE (Training In DEployment), a human-in-the-loop online post-training system. TIDE introduces a provenance-conditioned supervised learning framework that updates the policy online from human interventions and policy-generated rollouts collected during deployment, without a learned critic, reward model, or action scorer. Across four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks, TIDE improves milestone-normalized task progress and binary full-task completion over the warm-start policy and matched additional offline demonstrations, and performs comparably to the fixed-policy collection baseline while making updated checkpoints available during deployment. Each task-specific online post-training session, from the start of deployment rollouts until the final checkpoint is available, completes in less than one hour while learning and checkpoint handling run asynchronously.

documents.abstract: The activity-based care (ABC) model, adapted from activity-based offices, has emerged as a new approach to healthcare facility design. Evidence on its consequences for occupational health and safety-relevant outcomes remains limited. The study examines how transitioning from a traditional hospital design to the ABC model is associated with changes in employee experiences of task–environment alignment and psychosocial work environment, self-reported health, sick leave and turnover over time, and differences in changes across professional roles and clinic types. A repeated-measures survey was conducted in an outpatient hospital unit across 10 specialised clinics. Data were collected 3 months before relocation and at 6 and 18 months post-relocation. Generalised least-squares models examined change over time and tested interactions with professional role and clinic type. Sick leave and turnover were analysed over approximately 1 year before and after relocation using segmented interrupted time-series regression. Ratings of task–environment alignment varied across clinic types and professional roles. Consultation-based clinics and physicians and administrative employees showed persistent declines over time, while surgical/radiology clinics and nursing roles remained stable or improved. Stress and recovery indicators worsened similarly across all groups. Psychosocial conditions were stable, though job satisfaction, perceived quality of work and referral intentions declined. Turnover remained unchanged, while sick leave varied across contexts and roles. The consequences of ABC implementation are not uniform but depend on the alignment of the redesigned workspace and the task demands of different clinical settings and professional groups, a contingency that cannot be easily detected with single time-point post-occupancy evaluation.

documents.abstract: In online higher education, discontinuities in student performance and socialization function as early signs of academic delay or dropout. This article presents an institutional pilot that integrated generative AI (TECgpt/Skill Studio) as technopedagogical support for an academic status assessment tool (VEA), used to detect at-risk trajectories in an online degree program. An ecosystem of five configurable assistants was designed to generate reports at the student, cohort, and program levels. It was evaluated using a qualitatively dominant methodology with the academic management team across four cohorts (N = 198 active students). Results indicate that the tool systematized the process and improved traceability, although output variability was observed and recommendations lacked sufficient differentiation. The tool provides value by standardizing and scaling academic support without replacing human mediation.

Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled cloud services are increasingly embedded in users' daily activities, yet little is known about how user stickiness develops in virtualized service environments. Drawing on process virtualization theory, uses and gratifications theory, and switching costs, this study examines how process virtualization capability shapes user stickiness through sociability gratification and usage gratification. Survey data from 443 AI cloud service users were analyzed using structural equation modeling. Results show that process virtualization capability positively affects both forms of gratification, which increase user stickiness. Switching costs weaken the effect of sociability gratification on stickiness but do not significantly moderate the effect of usage gratification. The study extends research on AI cloud services by distinguishing social and functional gratification pathways to user stickiness and showing how their sensitivity to switching costs differs.

documents.abstract: Firms that sell to other firms on credit now face a new design choice. Software agents built on large language models can gather evidence, draft credit memos, release held orders and chase overdue invoices. Yet there is little guidance on how much of this work an agent should do without a person. Most research on artificial intelligence in credit asks how accurate a model is, and most of it studies consumer lending. It says little about the decision rights of autonomous agents in business-to-business trade credit, where much activity sits outside consumer-protection and bank model-risk rules. This conceptual paper addresses that gap. It integrates research on trade credit, credit scoring, language-model agents, levels of automation, agency theory and model-risk governance. From this synthesis it builds the Verifiability-Weighted Autonomy framework. The central claim is simple: the autonomy granted to an agent should rise with the verifiability of the evidence behind a decision and fall with the decision's financial exposure and irreversibility. The paper defines four autonomy tiers and a transparent allocation rule. It maps twelve common trade-credit decisions onto the tiers. It proposes a Propose–Verify–Dispose architecture in which language-model agents propose, deterministic checks verify, and policy rules or people dispose. It offers seven testable propositions and four measures for future empirical work. For managers, the framework turns a vague question, "can we trust the agent?", into a concrete design rule that fits existing delegation-of-authority practice. Keywords: large language model agents; trade credit; delegation of authority; model risk management; human oversight

Developing emotional intelligence (EI) in higher education requires innovative pedagogical approaches supported by objective assessment methods. This study evaluated the effectiveness of an immersive virtual reality (VR) dance intervention for enhancing EI among Chinese university students by integrating motion analysis, physiological measurements, and computational modeling. A randomized controlled trial involving 145 participants was conducted over an eight-week intervention period. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: immersive VR dance training using head-mounted displays, two-dimensional (2D) screen-based dance instruction, or a control group receiving no practical training. Emotional intelligence was assessed using the Mayer–Salovey–Caruso Emotional Intelligence Test (MSCEIT) before the intervention, immediately afterward, and at a four-week follow-up. Motion kinematics, physiological indicators, and computational analyses were integrated to evaluate learning outcomes. In addition, an exploratory algorithmic personalization approach adapted the training protocol to individual participant characteristics. Participants in the VR group demonstrated an average improvement of 18.5 MSCEIT points (Cohen’s d = 1.68) together with a 34.2% increase in movement amplitude. Improvements in the 2D group were substantially smaller (7.3 points; d = 0.51), while the control group showed only minimal gains (2.1 points). The exploratory personalization analysis suggested an additional 23% improvement in intervention effectiveness. At the four-week follow-up, participants retained 76.2% of the acquired gains.

As AI-based decision-support systems become increasingly embedded in physical education and coaching practice, agreement and disagreement between algorithmic advice and participants’ immediate scenario judgments have become important but theoretically underexamined features of human-AI collaboration. Grounded in a shared Judge-Advisor System paradigm, four scenario-based experiments (total N = 859) manipulated whether an experimentally presented AI recommendation was consistent or conflicting with each participant’s prior judgment and tested machine trust and collaborative decision-making self-efficacy as psychological pathways to self-reported collaborative adaptive responses. Psychological resilience and rationale provision were examined as study-specific boundary conditions. Conflict significantly reduced machine trust (Study 1, d = 1.061) and self-efficacy (Study 2, B = −0.687), and both measured mediators carried significant negative indirect associations with adaptive responses (Study 1, B = −0.428; Study 2, via trust B = −0.201, via self-efficacy B = −0.127). Psychological resilience attenuated the between-condition difference in self-efficacy in Study 3 (index of moderated mediation = 0.115). In Study 4, rationale provision moderated the condition-to-trust association, F (1, 239) = 11.348, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.045: the conflict effect was −0.811 in the black-box condition but −0.182 when a rationale was provided. The manipulation therefore concerns advice-judgment agreement rather than a direct experimental comparison of data-driven judgment with established experiential intuition. Because the scenarios did not establish objective recommendation accuracy, the moderation patterns are interpreted as changes in psychological response rather than as evidence that preserving trust or self-efficacy necessarily improves calibration, decision quality, or welfare.

We report a qualitative study spanning more than six months with upper-primary students (ages 9–12) in southern China using a local LLM (Doubao) for writing. Two interview waves with ten students (nine re-interviewed) and six teachers (three re-interviewed) reveal a set of recurring shifts in our focal cohort: from novelty to strategy, from anthropomorphic “companion/virtual teacher” to tool-like framing, and from quick unsticking to guarded use shaped by dependence, fairness, and exam-transfer Footnote1 concerns. Students valued speed and breadth but noted mechanical tone, age/style mismatch, and weak transfer to AI-free tests. We map a Control × Dependency framework and before/after transitions, and surface tensions around classroom norms and equity amid policy ambiguity and uneven AI literacy. We suggest process-visible, agency-preserving integration: sentence- and phrase-level provenance with mandatory micro-edits, task-specific scaffold ceilingsFootnote2, and process-anchored assessment schemes that explicitly factor in AI-use traces.

documents.abstract: Introduction Motivation is closely related to students' engagement in learning, yet the associations of intrinsic motivation (IM) and externally oriented motivation (EM) may differ depending on whether they are examined separately or simultaneously. This study examined their shared and unique associations with self-reported creative-process practices (CPP) and learning engagement (LE) among Chinese university art students. Methods Survey data were collected from 481 students enrolled in art programs in one Chinese province using purposive sampling. Confirmatory factor analysis was used to evaluate the four-factor measurement model, followed by structural equation modeling of three specifications: an IM-only model, an EM-only model, and a simultaneous IM-EM model. Results When examined separately, both IM and EM were positively associated with CPP and LE and showed significant indirect associations with LE through CPP. When modeled simultaneously, IM retained significant associations with CPP and LE, whereas the corresponding EM associations and its indirect association through CPP were smaller and no longer statistically significant. The CPP-LE association remained positive and statistically significant across all three model specifications. Discussion The findings indicate that externally oriented motivation can show meaningful associations when considered independently, but much of this association may overlap with intrinsic motivational variance. They also highlight the importance of distinguishing separate from unique motivational associations and of treating creative-process practices and learning engagement as related but conceptually distinct aspects of creative learning.

Generative AI models are capable of generating human-like content, such as large language models (LLMs) generate texts. To automate processes, certain requirements regarding trustworthiness and correctness are fulfilled. To relieve people from controlling the created content, a concept known as LLM-as-a-judge is available. In this scenario, another instance of an LLM is prompted to act as a judge, and check the generated content for certain quality requirements. However, such a judgement might not always align with a human judgement. Besides noise and errors in the human judgement, another reason is just the fact that different human evaluators can have different opinions about the evaluation. One reason could be that there might be no universal or unequivocal assessment since it is challenging to formulate objective rules. This natural existence of variance in human judgement defines the best possible benchmark level of alignment for a model judge. In this work, a method is presented to calculate this best possible benchmark under variance in human judgement. By comparing the distribution of the deviations between human judgement with the distribution of the deviation between model and human judgement with statistical means allows defining a model judge as good enough. Thus, a pragmatic way is provided to decide whether human judgement for a specific task can reliably be automated by a model judge in the quality that we can expect from the corresponding human judges. The code and prompts of the analysis performed are available under https://github.com/Ocean-code-1995/llm-judge-good-enough .

Asked what to study, which career to pursue, or what product to build, large language models (LLMs) often recommend AI-related options. We ask where this tendency comes from by comparing models before and after fine-tuning and by varying how questions are asked. First, pretrained models already include explicit AI/ML terms in the recommendations of 27% of their responses, and their released instruction-tuned versions do so in 59%. Second, fine-tuning models ourselves shows that this rise is not inevitable: general instruction tuning leaves the rate unchanged, but removing the 7% of instruction examples that concern AI cuts it by 14 percentage points, below the level of the pretrained models it starts from. Data rewarding helpfulness raise it by 9 points, while data ranked by the preferences of diverse simulated users lower it by 9. Finally, with models held fixed, asking for the "best" option or for what to do "right now" raises the rate by 8 and 18 points, whereas telling the model it is an AI advisor adds 4. Overall, the tendency starts in pretraining, and what models learn afterward, together with how a question is phrased, decides how strongly it appears.

documents.abstract: Personal intelligence systems are taking on increasingly complex everyday tasks, yet repeated questions, unnecessary confirmations, and unwanted outreach can turn capable assistance into interaction burden. Reducing this burden requires agents to remember how users want to be assisted. However, existing memory benchmarks focus on factual recall and personalized answers and rarely test how agents learn and act on interaction preferences. We introduce MemPABench, an interactive environment for on-policy evaluation of memory in personal agents. MemPABench poses long-horizon tasks requiring agents to decide when to clarify, confirm, or act autonomously. Four grounded simulated users hold 14 preferences across work and personal contexts. Their feedback spans 99 sessions over four months, with five event-driven changes per user testing memory updates. We evaluate preference selection, delivered behavior, and sensitivity to context and preference change. Evaluating four memory systems across four LLM backbones, we find that current memory brings limited gains in preference selection. Retrieval-based systems (i.e. Mem0, MemOS, simple RAG) do not outperform No Memory, while File-based memory improves accuracy but applies preferences beyond relevant contexts. Our analysis shows that current memory struggles to retrieve interaction preferences and adapt to preference changes. Even with the correct preference available, overriding the agent's default interaction habits remains challenging. The environment and dataset are available at https://mempabench.com.

Human–robot interaction (HRI) failures remain a major barrier to deploying robots in real-world environments. Prior work often treats failures as isolated technical faults or focuses on post-hoc recovery behaviors. In practice, many breakdowns arise because humans and robots operate under inconsistent assumptions about the current world state. We propose WSM-Aware HRI, an IoT-enhanced modular framework that unifies diverse HRI breakdowns as World-State Mismatches (WSMs) between a human's instruction-implied assumptions and a robot's grounded world model built from multimodal perception and digital augmentation. A Large Language Model (LLM) is used to make implicit assumptions explicit, map them to a small set of mismatch types, and specify the evidence needed for verification against the robot's world state. WSM-Aware HRI shifts failure handling from execution-time recovery to proactive mismatch detection during intention formation, enabling interventions guided by safety, norm compliance, and multi-user coordination with transparent explanations. We evaluate mismatch identification in ten everyday cases spanning both visual and latent-state mismatches. The system can accurately produce the expected output results, and ablations show that reliable identification depends on appropriate grounding representations and verification-oriented refinement. These results indicate that treating interaction breakdowns as explicit world–state mismatches enables earlier detection of impending failures and offers a principled mechanism for integrating external evidence and social constraints into human–robot interaction.

ObjectiveEvaluate the sensitivity of eye-tracking metrics to variations in mental workload in rail traffic control, and how they may be modulated by operator experience.BackgroundRail traffic control is a safety-critical domain characterized by high cognitive demands. While subjective workload measures are widely used, objective, real-time indicators, particularly eye-tracking metrics, remain underexplored.MethodEighteen professional rail traffic controllers (9 novice, 9 experienced) performed a simulation-based experiment involving four different scenarios with varying traffic density and task complexity, while wearing a head-mounted eye tracker. Measures of gaze behavior and visual strategies (fixations in different areas of interest (AOI)) were computed, and compared to subjective workload measures, to assess the effects of task difficulty and experience.ResultsSome measures like pupil dilation showed substantial changes (by ∼100%), while others like stationary gaze entropy showed more modest changes (∼40%), with increased task demand. Measures such as fixation rate revealed significant interaction effects with experience, indicating distinct visual strategies of novices vs. experts. Compared to experts, novices relied more on global overview displays under higher workload, and reduced planning-related information use, as revealed by AOI analysis. Subjective workload measures corroborated with increases in perceived demand.ConclusionThis study advances mental workload assessment in rail traffic control by demonstrating that eye-tracking metrics are sensitive to workload variations, and also reveal underlying cognitive strategies unique to expertise.ApplicationThese findings support the development of real-time workload monitoring systems and inform training interventions focused on information integration and cognitive strategies in rail traffic control operations.

The increasing complexity of Industrial Control Systems (ICS) and their integration with IT infrastructures has significantly expanded the cyber threat landscape. Traditional cybersecurity models, primarily based on the Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA triad), fail to capture the broader societal and operational impacts of cyberattacks. This paper proposes a novel framework that integrates Digital Twin technology with a Cyber-Social Security model to simulate, analyze, and quantify cyber threats in critical infrastructures. Virtualized ICS environments built with Mininet and MiniCPS are used to model attack scenarios and assess their consequences across technical and social dimensions. At the core of the framework lies the Cyber-Social Vulnerability Scoring System (CSVSS), a quantitative metric that extends CVSS with a Social Impact dimension grounded in the Entity and Place pillars, producing a single, reproducible severity score that reflects real-world consequences. Crucially, the framework does not automate risk assessment but keeps the human analyst at its center: a Large Language Model (LLM) performs a first-pass analysis, mapping vulnerabilities and drafting risk reports, while the analyst, supported by explainable AI feedback, validates the findings and retains decision authority over critical cases. Experimental results demonstrate the framework's ability to model and score cyber-social impact, while the human-in-the-loop design is presented as a conceptual principle to preserve oversight.

As artificial intelligence moves beyond answering questions and begins acting on our behalf, institutions face two connected problems. People may retain formal authority while losing the practical conditions needed to exercise judgment. Meanwhile, AI systems can carry out technically correct actions without legitimate authorization. This manifesto argues for human agency, legitimate institutional authority, and accountable action. It examines meaningful human oversight, the limits of delegated authority, verification when actions produce consequences, and the obligations of those who govern AI. Its guiding principle, Authority Before Autonomy, calls for responsible delegation without surrendering the capacity to question, correct, and answer for what follows.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being considered for Human Resource Management (HRM), including recruitment, employee selection, training and development, performance management, employee engagement, and workforce planning. This paper reviews the applications, potential benefits, challenges, and ethical considerations associated with AI in HRM. The study follows a descriptive approach based on secondary sources, including academic literature and professional reports. The review suggests that AI may support routine tasks, organize workforce information, and assist HR decisionmaking. However, privacy, algorithmic bias, implementation costs, accuracy, technical knowledge, and employee trust remain important concerns. The paper concludes that AI should support rather than replace human judgement, with responsible policies, data protection, and appropriate human supervision.

documents.abstract: Purpose Universities are increasingly adopting institutional policies on academic integrity (AcI) and artificial intelligence (AI), but it remains unclear whether these expectations are translated coherently into the course-level documents that govern students’ learning and assessment. This article therefore examines how AcI and AI, including generative AI (GenAI), are articulated in official teaching guides for Spain’s Master’s Degree in Teacher Training, and whether guidance is embedded coherently across course design. Design/methodology/approach A documentary content analysis was conducted on 254 publicly available guides from 68 universities. Explicit AcI and AI references were coded across objectives, competencies, learning outcomes, activities and assessment. Two formative diagnostic indices measured breadth of coverage across these five sections. Mann–Whitney tests compared university and subject types; 25% of the corpus was independently double-coded. Findings AcI was mentioned in 53.5% of guides but was concentrated in assessment and competencies; 46.5% contained no valid reference. Explicit AI guidance remained marginal (6.3%) and primarily assessment-centred. Private universities showed slightly broader AcI coverage, public universities slightly broader AI coverage and Final Master’s Project guides substantially broader AcI coverage. Research limitations/implications The indices measure documentary breadth, not the quality, depth or implementation of guidance, and guides are nested within universities. Practical implications Programme leaders should integrate task-specific integrity and AI expectations across outcomes, activities, assessment, disclosure and formative support, with attention to future teachers’ professional AI literacy. Originality/value The study provides a large-scale, programme-specific audit and a transparent method for benchmarking cross-sectional curricular integration without treating document coverage as a quality score.

The shift to agentic AI represents a major paradigm change in the field of intelligent systems research and development, as these systems are capable of establishing sub-goals, planning for a goal, and executing plans with only minimal human oversight. This capability offers a unique chance to promote gender equality, inclusive digital engagement, and sustainable growth via evolving, accessible and fair AI-based methods throughout industries. Meanwhile, the increased autonomy of agentic AI systems presents unique challenges such as the potential for algorithmic bias to be amplified, decision-making disparities, and a lack of governance, each of which requires responsible AI, transparent governance, and clear ethical frameworks. This paper presents a systematic literature review and bibliometric analysis of a 41 paper corpus from Scopus. The review follows PRISMA 2020 guidelines and summarizes the evidence regarding agentic and generative AI architectures, typologies of bias, and sectoral applications in healthcare, education, and gender equity. The paper presents a human-centred conceptual framework for responsible governance of agentic AI, building on lifecycle-governance and equity-by-design approaches, which merges bias mitigation, gender-inclusive design, and sustainability transition. The network of co-authorship is highly fragmented (density = 0.021; number of components = 37 from 88 authors), suggesting that there is no coordinated research agenda and giving empirical support to the integrative framework proposed here. This fragmentation further indicates that the vision and capabilities of agentic AI to contribute to gender equality and education are still not fully explored in the context of governance and sustainability, highlighting the relevance of the framework introduced in this paper. documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping education, yet research remains fragmented across technological streams and often conflates technical capability with demonstrated educational effectiveness. This narrative review synthesizes representative literature published mainly between 2010 and 2026 to trace the evolution of AI-enabled education from computer-assisted instruction toward adaptive, immersive, generative, and potentially more general forms of intelligence. It compares three major technological streams: intelligent tutoring and adaptive learning systems, extended reality (XR), and large language model-based generative AI. The review finds that intelligent tutoring systems support learner modeling, adaptive feedback, and personalization, but their evidence base is methodologically heterogeneous. XR shows comparatively more consolidated evidence, particularly through systematic reviews and meta-analyses, with generally positive but context-dependent effects on engagement and learning outcomes. Generative AI expands dialogic explanation, scaffolding, content generation, and personalized support, although learner-outcome evidence remains limited relative to capability benchmarking. Building on these findings, the review proposes a Technology–Mechanism–Outcome–Challenge framework and argues that future progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) should be evaluated through learning mechanisms, measurable outcomes, human oversight, equity, and responsible governance.

Adoption of artificial intelligence in K-12 schools has outpaced guidance for students, teachers, and administrators. Existing AI-literacy frameworks emphasize understanding and use; cybersecurity frameworks predate AI-specific threats, and neither defines AI security literacy as a competency domain in its own right. We propose an AI Security Literacy (AISL) framework of six dimensions spanning the school ecosystem, ground its technical dimensions in public AI-safety benchmarks and a reproducible multi-seed adversarial evaluation, and ground its attitudinal dimensions in nationally representative survey micro-data from U.S. teachers and adults. Only 34.5% of teachers report a school AI policy, and teachers see their own AI use as easing their work but students' use as complicating it; on the technical side, a reported robustness figure depends as much on the attack and the particular trained model as on the system evaluated. NeuralFortify, a browser-based K-12 platform built on real AI models, is presented as an illustrative operationalization.

The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), including generative AI, natural language processing, machine learning and automated data-analysis systems, is transforming the production and dissemination of financial news. In Nigeria, where journalists increasingly rely on digital tools to interpret corporate disclosures, analyse financial statements and communicate market information to investors and the wider public, AI-assisted financial journalism presents both opportunities and credibility risks. This article examines the relationship between AI-assisted financial journalism and the credibility of corporate financial information in Nigeria. The study adopts an integrative literature-review approach, drawing on recent scholarly literature published between 2024 and 2026. The review is anchored on Source Credibility Theory, Technology Acceptance Model, Diffusion of Innovations Theory, Information Asymmetry Theory and Gatekeeping Theory. Seven recent empirical studies were critically reviewed, including studies of Nigerian journalists' AI adoption, newsroom practices, AI-attributed news credibility, AI disclosure and automated data-driven journalism. The review indicates that AI can improve the speed, analytical capacity, consistency and accessibility of financial journalism, particularly where journalists use AI to process large corporate datasets, identify anomalies, summarise reports and generate preliminary financial stories. However, the credibility benefits are not automatic. Risks arise from hallucinated information, inaccurate numerical interpretation, algorithmic bias, inadequate disclosure, overdependence on automated outputs, weak verification and the cultural and linguistic limitations of AI systems operating in Nigerian contexts. Recent Nigerian evidence also indicates that journalists are increasingly using AI for transcription, editing and preliminary drafting, while human journalists continue to retain important editorial responsibilities. The article argues that the credibility of AI-assisted financial journalism depends less on automation itself than on the quality of human verification, source transparency, professional competence, data provenance and institutional governance surrounding AI use. The article proposes a Human–AI Financial Journalism Credibility Framework in which AI performs computational and assistive functions while journalists retain responsibility for verification, interpretation, contextualisation and ethical publication. The study contributes to emerging literature by connecting AI-assisted journalism with the credibility of corporate financial information in an African emerging-market context.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to automate and optimize software testing, but the evidence is distributed across heterogeneous testing activities, AI techniques, and evaluation measures. This study maps AI-driven software-testing research and translates the evidence into capabilities relevant to a Test Center of Excellence (TCoE). A systematic evidence workflow was applied to a unified audit corpus of 2,072 records, followed by focused eligibility reconciliation and full-text verification. The final focused evidence workset contains 29 records: 15 primary empirical studies, 9 secondary studies, 1 scope exclusion, and 4 full-text/access exclusions. The primary evidence covers machine learning, reinforcement learning, evolutionary and search-based methods, deep learning, explainable AI, and large language models. The supported testing activities include test generation, selection and prioritization, minimization and optimization, fuzzing, validation, adaptive automation, and maintenance. The synthesis shows that AI should be treated in a TCoE as a governed capability layer rather than as a single automation tool. The proposed capability model links AI techniques to testing activities, measurable outcomes, reusable TCoE capabilities, and governance with human oversight. The study also identifies gaps in reliability, context awareness, test-oracle support, long-term maintenance, CI/CD integration, reproducibility, and standardized evaluation.

Abstract This working paper introduces AI-Native Organizational Architecture (ANOA), a theoretical framework for the structural transformation of enterprises and institutions operating in an increasingly autonomous computational economy. The research examines the limitations of conventional hierarchical organizations when artificial intelligence reduces information-processing and execution costs while introducing new challenges in coordination, institutional authority, accountability, and verification. ANOA proposes five interconnected organizational functions: Design, Human Authority, Orchestration, Execution, and Independent Assurance. Rather than establishing a rigid hierarchy, the framework separates architectural responsibility, legitimate decision authority, computational coordination, authorized execution, and independent verification. The paper develops mathematical hypotheses concerning computational productivity, architectural capital, organizational complementarities, coordination costs, and risk-adjusted economic value. It also introduces Architectural Value Participation (AVP), a proposed contractual mechanism linking compensation to independently attributable architectural contributions. The educational extension, ANOA-E, explores AI-native learning environments in which students interact directly with supervised large language models, formulate questions, critically evaluate explanations, and demonstrate independent reasoning. Philosophical judgment, practical wisdom, and accountable human authority are examined as complementary foundations for AI-native organizational governance. The study presents comparative organizational models, formal delegation mechanisms, falsifiable hypotheses, and a proposed empirical research agenda. ANOA is presented as a conceptual and testable framework rather than an empirically established organizational standard. Keywords: AI-Native Organizations; Organizational Architecture; Computational Economics; Human Authority; AI Governance; Architectural Capital; Organizational Productivity; Agentic AI; Verifiable Delegation; Architectural Value Participation; AI-Native Education; Critical Thinking. Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being incorporated into higher education and foreign language instruction, offering opportunities for personalized feedback, adaptive learning materials, multimodal content delivery, and individualized learning support. However, the extent to which these opportunities translate into equitable learning experiences for university students with disabilities remains insufficiently understood, particularly in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) classroom in developing educational contexts.

Abstract This paper introduces a thought experiment in reverse alignment, in which, instead of aligning artificial intelligence (AI) with human values, we examine how humans inadvertently align with AI systems. We posit a theoretically perfect AI assistant and demonstrate that even this idealized system can produce concerning dynamics. In particular, we build on principles from pattern reinforcement and behavioral inertia to intuitively show that as the quality of AI assistance increases, human decision making tends to converge toward a utility-tilted sharpening of the assistant’s predictive distribution. Critically, this convergence exhibits strong path dependence: withdrawing assistance does not, by itself, restore cognitive independence, because the update contains no force that returns an agent to its pre-assistance policy. Recovery requires an active novelty incentive, and even then, it proceeds through history-dependent transients whose duration can exceed institutional planning horizons. We formalize these dynamics through two lenses: the Alice-Bob divergence , which tracks how adoption timing alone creates persistent cognitive divergence between identical agents, and the Three Inevitabilities , which captures the multi-scale forces (i.e. individual, social, and species-level) that drive convergence. Our theoretical and mathematical analysis reveals a fundamental trilemma: systems cannot simultaneously maintain optimal task outcomes, persistent human cognitive independence, and the absence of artificial novelty incentives. We conclude by identifying escape mechanisms and interventions that preserve human agency while retaining beneficial AI assistance to navigate the tension between augmentation and autonomy.

documents.abstract: Educational feedback generated by artificial intelligence is becoming more and more popular in teaching, but there are still differences in how to evaluate its quality in existing research. This study examined 68 empirical studies and compared the criteria, methods, evaluators, and evidence used in these evaluations. The results show that the relevant evaluation can be roughly summarised into three dimensions: Evidence Validity, Rubric and Task Alignment, and Pedagogical Usefulness. Evidence Validity focuses on whether the feedback is accurate and reliable, and is based on the learner's actual work. Rubric and Task Alignment focuses on whether the feedback meets the task requirements, evaluation criteria, and learner responses. Pedagogical Usefulness focuses on whether the feedback is clear, specific, actionable, and can support revision and further learning. The reviewed studies also used a variety of evidence to judge the quality of feedback, including human judgement, learner perceptions, revision behaviour, learning outcomes, and automated metrics. Based on these findings, this study proposes an evaluation framework that links different dimensions of feedback quality with corresponding evidence to provide clearer evaluation ideas for subsequent research and educational practice.

documents.abstract: Artificial Emotional Intelligence (AEI) refers to Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems that mediate human affect by sensing, processing, and responding to emotional states through multimodal inputs, including text, voice, and physiological signals (Chen et al. 2024 ). As AI systems (especially generative AI) become more conversational, personalised, and multimodal, AEI increasingly mediates therapy, companionship, customer service, education, and work (De Freitas et al. 2026 ; Zao-Sanders 2026 ). This marks a shift from mediating information and behaviour to mediating affect in sensitive contexts: AEI already underpins chatbots designed to mitigate suicide risk (Maples et al. 2024 ), customer-service systems that respond to frustration (Fan et al. 2024 ), and personalised sexbot applications (Rubinsztein and Ciriello 2024 ). This shift reflects technical progress, but also intensifies concerns about social fragmentation, care-capacity gaps, and the expansion of monetisation-oriented platform logics into domains historically organised around care, trust, and professional duty (Arsel 2026 ; Leong et al. 2021 ; Seleznova et al. 2023 ). Despite its significance, this reconfiguration of digital intermediation remains under-conceptualised in Information Systems (IS) research.

documents.abstract: This study aims to deepen the understanding of artificial intelligence's (AI) impact on work by introducing and describing the AI-Job Dynamics Framework. Drawing from sociotechnical systems theory, complexity theory, and organizational learning theories, we conceptualize AI integration as a dynamic, non-linear process with three key phases. The framework, supported by theoretical propositions, identifies how this process affects organizational decision-making structures and key job characteristics over time, emphasizing the balance between centralization and decentralization of decision-making power. AI integration initially reduces job autonomy but may lead to greater autonomy in later phases as AI becomes more embedded. Throughout this process, AI reshapes skill requirements from routine to complex cognitive and adaptive skills. In the advanced phase of AI integration, we introduce the alternative paths and varied trajectories through which AI, organizational structures, and individual work experiences evolve. We conclude by discussing the implications of this framework for future research on AI and job design.

Employee retention has become a strategic concern for commercial enterprises because avoidable turnover can increase recruitment costs, disrupt organizational knowledge, and weaken workforce continuity. This study develops an integrated decision-support framework linking artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled human resource practices, predictive analytics capability, employee data quality, AI-supported career development, organizational support for AI, employee engagement, and employee retention. The framework follows a quantitative survey design and combines descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, exploratory factor analysis, correlation, multiple regression, mediation analysis, PLS-SEM-oriented measurement assessment, and machine-learning validation. A dataset of 250 responses is used only to demonstrate the structure and presentation of statistical analysis; it is not claimed to represent actual field observations. The results indicate acceptable internal consistency, positive associations among the principal constructs, significant predictive relationships, and stronger predictive performance for nonlinear machine-learning models than the regression baseline. The study positions AI and predictive analytics not as replacements for managerial judgement but as decisionsupport mechanisms for identifying retention risks, targeting interventions, and improving evidence-based workforce planning.

Large language models (LLMs) showed greater accuracy than traditional machine learning (ML) models for classifying crime incidents, particularly when the LLMs were fine-tuned using policing data. LLMs also showed greater accuracy in understanding the context and meaning of written crime reports, making crime analysis more efficient and accurate. All artificial intelligence (AI) technologies used for policing purposes should be implemented cautiously, with human oversight, transparency, and safeguards against biased training data to prevent discriminatory policing outcomes.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been at the forefront of technological developments influencing business research. Advances in machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, predictive analytics and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have enabled researchers to process increasingly complex data, automate analytical tasks and generate deeper insights. This study conducts a critical review of the evolution, applications, opportunities and challenges of AI in business research. Drawing upon contemporary literature from management, marketing, strategy, innovation, operations, finance and human resource management, the review synthesises knowledge regarding AI-driven decision-making, predictive analytics and knowledge creation. The review finds that AI improves research efficiency and supports evidence-based managerial decision-making. However, the literature highlights significant concerns relating to algorithmic bias, explainability, transparency, privacy, governance and research integrity. Existing scholarship is fragmented across disciplines and provides limited empirical evidence regarding the long-term implications of generative AI for research quality, organisational learning, governance effectiveness and human-AI collaboration. The study argues that AI should be viewed as a complementary capability that augments rather than replaces human expertise. By integrating evidence across multiple business functions, the review identifies critical knowledge gaps and develops a future research agenda focused on responsible governance, explainable AI and sustainable human-AI collaboration.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a transformative force that is reshaping educational systems, pedagogical approaches, and learning environments. Similar to the impact of the Industrial Revolution on the development of mass education, the AI revolution has led to a fundamental reconsideration of educational objectives, teaching methods, curriculum structures, and the roles of teachers and students. Traditional educational models were largely teacher-centered and based on standardized curricula in which students acted as passive recipients of knowledge. In contrast, contemporary knowledge societies emphasize critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, problem-solving, and lifelong learning skills. In this context, AI technologies have accelerated the transition toward more learner-centered and personalized educational models. Subfields such as machine learning, natural language processing, and big data analytics have increasingly entered educational environments through intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment tools, virtual assistants, and adaptive learning platforms. Applications such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Khan Academy’s Khanmigo illustrate the growing role of AI in teaching and learning processes. While these technologies provide significant opportunities for personalization, accessibility, and learning efficiency, they also raise ethical and social concerns related to data privacy, digital inequality, and academic integrity. This article systematically examines the historical and theoretical foundations of artificial intelligence in education and analyzes the evolving roles of teachers and students within AI-supported learning environments. Furthermore, the study evaluates the opportunities and challenges associated with AI integration and presents policy-oriented and practical recommendations for the ethical and effective implementation of AI technologies in education.

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: This study investigates the perceived barriers to integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into nursing education among nurse educators and nursing students at a public higher education institution in Gauteng, South Africa. Methods: A qualitative, exploratory, descriptive, contextual design was employed. Purposive sampling was used to recruit 12 nurse educators and 28 third-year nursing students. Data collection was conducted through semi-structured interviews with nurse educators and focus group discussions with nursing students. The data were analysed thematically, utilising Braun and Clarke’s six-phase framework, with the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology(UTAUT) serving as an interpretative lens. Results: Four interrelated barriers emerged: infrastructure and resource constraints; limited AI literacy and skills; resistance and readiness challenges; and governance, ethical, and regulatory concerns. These barriers collectively influenced participants' willingness and capacity to engage with AI in nursing education. Conclusions: The effective integration of AI into nursing education necessitates coordinated institutional responses that address infrastructure, AI literacy, organisational readiness, and ethical governance. Developing contextually relevant policies, ensuring equitable access to technology, providing continuous professional development, and offering appropriate technical support may foster a more conducive environment for the responsible and sustainable integration of AI into nursing education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence literacy is increasingly important in nursing education, but it remains unclear how its dimensions relate to three constructs related to the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM): perceived usefulness (PU), perceived ease of use (PEU) and attitudes toward artificial intelligence (ATU). This study aimed to examine these relationships and to identify factors associated with artificial intelligence literacy. Methods A multi-institutional cross-sectional study surveyed first-year nursing students at six undergraduate institutions in one province of China from 20 April to 1 May 2026. Of 375 questionnaire submissions, 362 met the quality-control criteria and were analysed (analytic retention rate: 96.5%). Separate item-level confirmatory factor analyses evaluated the four-factor literacy structure and the distinctiveness of PU, PEU and ATU. Group comparisons and multivariable regression with heteroscedasticity-robust inference examined correlates of overall artificial intelligence literacy; Pearson correlations described pairwise associations. A regularised partial correlation network mapped conditional relationships, centrality and bridge connectivity among seven dimension-mean nodes: knowledge, skills, values, ethics, PU, PEU and ATU. Between-institution differences, clustering and robustness of pooled findings were assessed. Results In the fully adjusted multivariable model, more frequent artificial intelligence use, prior artificial intelligence education and interest in artificial intelligence were positively associated with the mean artificial intelligence literacy score. The four-factor model showed good fit and strong item loadings; skills and values were highly correlated. Measurement analyses supported PU, PEU and ATU as correlated but distinguishable constructs. Of 21 potential network edges, 17 were non-zero. Skills had the highest expected influence and PU the highest strength. One-step bridge rankings were partition-dependent: values ranked first under the primary two-community partition and PU under the alternative four-community partition; PEU ranked second in both. Bootstrap diagnostics supported strong stability of strength and expected influence under case removal (CS(cor = 0.7) = 0.751 for both). Intraclass correlation estimates were near zero; institution-adjusted analyses preserved the main regression and network findings. Conclusions Artificial intelligence use frequency, prior artificial intelligence education and interest were positively associated with artificial intelligence literacy. Skills, perceived usefulness, values and perceived ease of use may inform hypotheses for prospective evaluation of artificial intelligence education in undergraduate nursing programmes.

documents.abstract: AIM: To examine how artificial intelligence literacy, self-efficacy and perceptions and attitudes relate to artificial intelligence acceptance among nutrition and dietetics students, practising dietitians and academics in Türkiye. METHODS: A cross-sectional online survey was administered to 317 participants (98 undergraduate students, 139 dietitians, 80 academics) between February and August 2025 using validated scales. The model was tested with partial least squares structural equation modelling (5,000 bootstrap subsamples), specific indirect effects for mediation, and measurement invariance with permutation-based multi-group analysis. RESULTS: The model explained 56.4% of the variance in artificial intelligence acceptance. Positive perceptions and attitudes showed the strongest association with acceptance (β = 0.577, 95% confidence interval 0.399 to 0.725), whereas negative perceptions were unrelated to it (β = -0.026, p = 0.509). Artificial intelligence literacy was strongly linked to self-efficacy (β = 0.580) and related to acceptance largely indirectly (68.7% of its total effect), mainly through positive perceptions and self-efficacy. Self-efficacy was also associated with higher acceptance (β = 0.191) and weaker negative perceptions (β = -0.328). No structural path differed across the three groups after correction for multiple testing. CONCLUSIONS: Acceptance was associated less with negative perceptions than with artificial intelligence literacy, which related to acceptance through favourable perceptions and self-efficacy. Training combining hands-on artificial intelligence literacy with critical appraisal of artificial intelligence outputs may support informed adoption across career stages.

documents.abstract: Objective Hemorrhagic transformation (HT) is a major complication after mechanical thrombectomy (MT) in acute ischemic stroke (AIS). Although artificial intelligence (AI)-driven imaging-based prediction models have shown promise for predicting HT, their overall predictive performance remains uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated their predictive performance. Methods PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, and CBM/SinoMed were searched from inception to July 2, 2026. Studies developing or validating AI-driven imaging-based prediction models for predicting HT after MT in AIS, including both pre- and post-procedural imaging predictors, were included. A random-effects model was used to pool the area under the curve (AUC), while a bivariate random-effects model was used to jointly estimate pooled sensitivity and specificity and construct the SROC curve. Subgroup analyses explored potential sources of heterogeneity. Results Eleven studies (total N = 3,541) were included, 10 studies contributed eligible AUC estimates, with evaluation cohorts ranging from 18 to 261 participants. The pooled AUC was 0.891 (95% CI: 0.853–0.928), with low between-study heterogeneity ( I 2 = 29.0%, p = 0.238). The bivariate random-effects model yielded a pooled sensitivity of 0.666 (95% CI: 0.578–0.744) and a pooled specificity of 0.919 (95% CI: 0.842–0.960). Exploratory subgroup analyses did not provide robust evidence supporting the superiority of any specific subgroup, and their interpretation was limited by small subgroup sizes and methodological heterogeneity. However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the limited number of studies within individual subgroups. Conclusion AI-driven imaging-based prediction models showed generally favorable discrimination in predicting HT after MT in AIS. However, current evidence does not establish the superiority of any specific model type. The predominance of retrospective studies, limited external validation, and methodological heterogeneity limit the generalizability of current findings. Large, multicenter prospective studies with rigorous external validation are needed before clinical implementation. Systematic review registration The systematic review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261441463).

documents.abstract: Organizations increasingly invest in adopting digital technologies to improve efficiency and competitiveness. Yet, in the post-adoption phase, these benefits depend on continued employee–technology interaction in everyday work, which can shape employee work and wellbeing and thereby influence organizational performance. Little is known, however, about how organizations assess these implications. Drawing on sociotechnical systems and performance measurement perspectives, this multiple-case study examines post-adoption assessment practices in eight Finnish organizations. The findings reveal a post-adoption blind spot: information on technology performance and use, employee work, and wellbeing was addressed through disconnected practices, indirect proxies, and informal judgements. Respondents reported recurring problems that remained weakly captured by current assessment: tool fragmentation, continuous adaptation demands, uneven performance effects, and work intensification, reflected more broadly in efficiency erosion and technology-related stress. The study conceptualizes integrated performance measurement systems as a potential mechanism for institutionalizing sociotechnical feedback through joint, recurring review of technology- and employee-related information.
