Recursive self-improvement (RSI) promises AI systems, such as self-evolving LLM agents, that become better at producing further improvements. Evaluating this promise requires separating product claims about the final system from process claims about the improvement process itself. Existing surveys specify the evidence these claims require, but how often studies report that evidence remains unmeasured. We examine this question through full-text coding of 114 eligible studies in a reproducible arXiv search frame frozen in October 2026, including 90 that describe their own systems as RSI. The codebook links claims to evaluation designs. Independent human coding, third-reader adjudication, and a separate blind coding of improver comparisons assess coding reliability. Among the 90 RSI studies, 90% report product evaluation beyond development tasks under a broad criterion that includes partial or unstated separation, while 60% report evaluation on tasks unused for selection. Only 22% audit two or more reruns of the full loop. In a human-coded random sample, the RSI studies show the same contrast: 45% evaluate on tasks unused for selection and 14% audit two or more reruns. Of the 26 studies claiming a better improvement procedure, 23 report a related comparison, but only 4 compare earlier and later procedures from identical starting artifacts at a matched budget. Across these results and a comparison set of established works, evidence for repeatability and improved procedures remains less developed than product evaluation. Three propositions explain how selection effects, shared evaluator errors, and changes in system state limit what product evaluations can establish. Together, the findings support a claim-indexed reporting standard that connects each claim to the evaluation design needed to test it.

Large language model chatbots have been proposed as AI-interviewers for collecting qualitative interview data at scale, potentially bridging social science's longstanding divide between the breadth of surveys and the depth of qualitative interviews. This paper provides the first direct empirical comparison of data quality in AI-led and human-led interviews. In a randomized experiment (N = 41), university students were interviewed via synchronous text chat by either trained non-expert interviewers or a locally hosted AI system; we evaluate exposure, specificity, and relevance. Median interview duration was similar across conditions, but AI-interviewers asked more than twice as many questions per interview and elicited roughly 65 percent more respondent text per interview. Per-question responses were longer with human interviewers, though not after multiple-testing correction; only AI-condition participants skipped questions. Responses were almost uniformly on-topic in both conditions; for specificity we detect no difference, but the design cannot exclude one of up to three quarters of a point. These results were obtained with a small, locally hosted open-weight model (7B parameters), which addresses concerns about data security, GDPR compliance, and scientific reproducibility. Our findings support the viability of AI-interviewing for large-N qualitative data collection.

This article presents an applied analysis of civil protection measures and strategies applicable in the event of natural or anthropogenic disasters capable of damaging or destroying the built environment and endangering human lives, with particular focus on earthquakes and missile strikes. The study aims to systematically examine the phases of disaster preparedness, response, and recovery, evaluating risk assessment strategies, survivor search technologies, and emergency habitat solutions available in the current scientific and operational literature and practice. By synthesizing cross-disciplinary insights from architecture, engineering, emergency management, and artificial intelligence research, the article identifies key tools and methodologies that contribute to reducing vulnerability, optimizing resource use, and accelerating recovery. The analysis further highlights gaps in current approaches and proposes directions for improvement, including the scientific grounding of novel shelter proposals and implications for future civil protection policy.

When a language model develops capabilities not traceable to its individual components, when a multi-agent AI system outperforms each agent on its own, or when a human-AI pair succeeds where either fails in isolation, AI researchers describe it as a case of ``synergy'' or ``emergence''. However, these are usually informal assessments not supported by a theoretical framework, making these claims impossible to compare or even meaningfully dispute. Here we argue that \emph{information decomposition can serve as a unifying formal framework to operationalize assessments about synergy in AI systems}. Information decomposition provides a way to distinguish qualitatively different \emph{types} of information, including unique information available from individual components, redundant information shared across multiple components, and synergistic information accessible only from parts taken together. This gives claims of emergence a precise, falsifiable criterion: a system's behavior is emergent only if it carries synergistic information about task-relevant outcomes. We apply this lens to attention heads, autonomous agents, and human-AI teams, showing how it organizes existing knowledge across scales and substrates, while also generating cross-level conjectures that siloed fields would miss.

Prolonged computer use can change the workload and strain a person experiences, but these changes are hard to see in task output alone. This paper presents CognitoShield AI, a privacy-oriented platform that estimates stress-related behavioral signals and cognitive workload indicators from interaction timing. The implemented pipeline aggregates telemetry into 30-second observations, derives a seven-feature representation, and applies an XGBoost regression model. A personal-baseline signal and a bounded context-aware fusion stage add personalization, and a FastAPI backend with a web interface presents the estimates together with recovery-oriented guidance. On a synthetic held-out test set, the model reached a mean absolute error (MAE) of 10.29, a root mean square error of 13.15, and an R-squared value of 0.7916. In an exploratory check of nine real users, the production seven-feature model recorded an MAE of 35.2367, while the P7 and P13 variants recorded 35.6300 and 35.2644, respectively. These results are preliminary and cannot establish generalization or clinical validity. The design does not collect raw typed characters and uses no camera-based or facial analysis. CognitoShield AI is therefore offered as a behavioral estimation and self-awareness tool, not a diagnostic system.

With the development of aviation automation and artificial intelligence, Single-Pilot Operations (SPO) have gradually become an important research direction for future civil aviation. Compared with conventional dual-pilot operations, SPO reduces the number of pilots in the cockpit, but the original flight tasks do not disappear. Instead, these tasks need to be redistributed among the single pilot, automated systems, and necessary ground support. Therefore, mitigating pilot workload arising from such task redistribution constitutes a key challenge for the development of SPO. Based on existing studies, this paper compares conventional dual-pilot operations with intelligent-assisted SPO, with particular attention to relatively high-workload phases such as approach and landing. The comparison focuses on three aspects: task distribution and quantity, task difficulty and time pressure, and task sequence and interaction. Through these dimensions, the paper examines how changes in crew configuration and task redistribution affect pilot workload and further discusses the role of intelligent assistance in workload management under SPO. The analysis suggests that the transition from dual-pilot operations to SPO primarily changes the distribution of tasks and workload. Without sufficient assistance, a single pilot may experience greater workload because more tasks can become concentrated on one person. Intelligent assistance can take over some monitoring, information-processing, and support functions, allowing tasks and attentional resources to be distributed more effectively. However, existing evidence remains insufficient to establish that intelligent assistance necessarily reduces the overall workload of SPO below that of conventional dual-pilot operations. Therefore, the development of intelligent-assisted SPO should focus on effective human–automation task allocation rather than simply increasing the level of automation.

The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into higher education presents both significant opportunities and critical challenges for institutions in Africa and the wider Global South. While GenAI can expand access to information, support teaching and learning, and strengthen research productivity, its deployment also raises questions concerning whose knowledge is represented, which languages are privileged, how credibility is constructed, and who exercises control over the infrastructures and data on which artificial intelligence depends. This article critically examined the implications of these challenges through the lenses of decolonial theory, epistemic justice, African philosophical thought, and critical AI studies. Rather than treating artificial intelligence as a culturally neutral technological artefact, the article conceptualises AI as a sociotechnical system whose knowledge practices are shaped by historical, economic, linguistic and epistemological relations of power. Drawing on a critical interpretive synthesis of scholarly literature, policy documents and African philosophical perspectives, the article developed the Ubuntu-Ẹ̀kọ́ Framework as an original conceptual contribution. The framework brings together relationality, ethical character, contextual responsiveness, critical consciousness and communal capability. Building on this framework, the article proposes Augmented Collective Wisdom (ACW) as a reorientation of AI from a technology primarily designed to automate or individualise knowledge work toward a sociotechnical resource that supports collective learning, human judgement, cultural integrity and community wellbeing. The article further advanced Digital Sovereignty as a strategic alternative to a narrow discourse of AI readiness. It concluded that decolonising AI in higher education does not require rejection of technological innovation; rather, it requires institutions to develop the epistemic, cultural, linguistic, infrastructural and governance capacities necessary to determine how AI is designed, interpreted, deployed and evaluated within their own contexts.

documents.abstract: To develop a context-sensitive model of artificial intelligence (AI) enabled salutogenic leadership for Abadan Oil Refinery, integrating occupational well-being with the organizational requirements of digital transformation. This applied qualitative study integrated theoretical evidence with semi-structured interviews with 18 academic and organizational experts selected purposively for their knowledge of leadership, management, and AI applications. Audio-recorded interviews were transcribed verbatim and analyzed in ATLAS.ti using open, axial, and selective coding. Two independent coders reconciled disagreements through discussion; the reported Cohen’s kappa was 0.79. Preliminary categories were also reviewed by participating experts. The analysis generated 140 initial open codes and a six-category paradigm model. The model comprised causal conditions, intervening conditions, contextual conditions, strategies, a core phenomenon, and anticipated outcomes. Its core combined health-promoting and sustainable leadership, psychological coherence and occupational health, and readiness for human–AI collaboration. Causal conditions concerned leadership relationships, organizational and technological drivers, and attitudes toward technology. Contextual and intervening conditions encompassed health culture, job demands and resources, digital infrastructure, psychological capacities, and digital leadership. Strategies emphasized health support, stress management, leadership development, employee learning, and responsible technological adaptation. Anticipated outcomes concerned employee health and well-being, work attitudes and engagement, and sustainable organizational performance. The model frames AI as a resource for human decision-making within a health-promoting leadership approach. It provides an exploratory framework for refinery management rather than evidence that AI implementation improves health, safety, or productivity. The proposed relationships require prospective evaluation.

The development of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, particularly Generative AI, has created new opportunities for developing innovative, interactive, and contextual learning media. However, many Islamic Religious Education (IRE) teachers still have limited competencies in utilizing this technology as a learning medium while maintaining Islamic values. This Community Service Program (PKM) aimed to improve the competence of IRE teachers at SMP Negeri 35 Medan in utilizing Generative AI to develop creative, effective, and Islamic value-based learning media. The program employed a Participatory Action Learning approach consisting of needs identification, educational sessions, practical training, mentoring, and evaluation. The training involved demonstrations and hands-on practice using various Generative AI platforms, including ChatGPT, Canva AI, Gamma AI, and Microsoft Copilot, to develop teaching materials, presentations, assessment questions, and visual learning media based on Islamic values. The results indicated an improvement in participants' understanding of Generative AI, enhanced skills in developing digital learning media, and increased awareness of the ethical use of AI from an Islamic perspective. The teachers were able to produce learning media that were more engaging, interactive, contextual, and supportive of the implementation of the Merdeka Curriculum. This program contributed positively to improving teachers' digital literacy while strengthening the integration of technology and Islamic values in the IRE learning process.

Artificial intelligence can provide individualized movement information at a frequency that is difficult to achieve through teacher observation alone. This study examined whether AI-supported corrective feedback could strengthen adolescents' physical education self-efficacy while improving movement execution. Eighty-four students aged 13–15 completed an eight-week controlled experiment involving bodyweight squats, forward lunges, and countermovement jumps. The AI group received pose-estimation-based feedback generated with MediaPipe Pose Landmarker and OpenCV, whereas the control group received standardized teacher feedback. The AI group increased self-efficacy from 4.17 ± 0.62 to 5.39 ± 0.56 points, compared with 4.19 ± 0.60 to 4.66 ± 0.61 in the control group, producing a significant group × time interaction, F(1,82) = 42.31, p < .001, ηp² = .340. Movement scores increased from 64.1 ± 6.8 to 82.3 ± 5.7 in the AI group. Within the AI condition, movement-score improvement and feedback engagement jointly predicted post-intervention self-efficacy, adjusted R²=.487. The findings indicate that interpretable, attempt-specific AI feedback can make mastery progress more visible and support both technical learning and efficacy beliefs in adolescent physical education.

Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered mobile-assisted language learning (MALL) applications are transforming the traditional language learning paradigm by leveraging AI technologies to provide a more efficient, convenient, and personalized learning experience. Despite the integration of AI technologies into MALL applications, prior studies have overlooked the critical role of AI service quality in shaping learners’ learning satisfaction levels and performance within these applications. This study addresses this research gap by leveraging social support theory to develop a research model that examines how the AI service quality of AI-powered MALL applications influences social support, specifically informational, emotional, and appraisal support. These forms of support are further analyzed to determine their effects on learners’ learning satisfaction levels and performance. A total of 978 valid samples were collected from users of AI-powered MALL applications and analyzed using the partial least-squares method. The results indicate that AI service quality significantly enhances users’ perceptions of informational, emotional, and appraisal support. These forms of support positively influence learning satisfaction and learning performance. Furthermore, the mediation analysis revealed that informational, emotional, and appraisal support act as partial mediators in the relationships between AI service quality and learning satisfaction and between AI service quality and learning performance. This study contributes to the literature by revealing how AI service quality, social support, and learning satisfaction and performance interact in the context of AI-enabled MALL applications. We also offer practical insights for improving the user experience and maximizing the learning outcomes of AI-driven MALL applications.

Generative Artificial Intelligence (genAI) has become a large influence on students and teachers in the mathematics classroom. Specifically, researchers found that genAI tools could solve probability questions such as “What is the probability of drawing the Queen of Hearts from a standard deck of playing cards on the first try?” These researchers also stated that the genAI tools could not be trusted when solving, “Three cards are lying face down in front of me. Two are face cards, and there are no spades. No card is next to a card of the same color. What are the odds that the card on the left is the Queen of Hearts?” However, it is unclear whether that statement is true. Thus, we verified these findings by investigating four genAI tools (ChatGPT, Gemini, Co-Pilot, and Claude AI) on their ability to complete the identified probability task to determine when genAI can be trusted to perform probability calculation. Using the results of this investigation, we examined these genAI models using their responses and the predictions made by the genAI trainer. The investigation implies that developing mathematical validity requires intentional instruction, including teaching students how to compare genAI’s explanations, conducting GenAI Triangulation Process, cross-checking results using independent methods or alternative tools, and justifying whether an answer is mathematically sound.

documents.abstract: This article aims to analyze the relevance of cognitive development and comprehensive ethical education in the critical and responsible use of generative artificial intelligence, with the purpose of preventing and counteracting the potential dehumanizing consequences that could affect the human condition in the twenty-first century. From a theoretical-analytical approach, it argues for the need for early digital education that fosters intellectual development and prevents technology from becoming a source of dependency. It highlights that education constitutes a key tool to counter cognitive laziness and the improper use of intelligent systems by university students, to the detriment of their critical reasoning capacities. It concludes that understanding the relevance of brain development and its relationship with cognitive learning processes constitutes an essential foundation for the formation of critical thinking and for the adoption of a responsible ethical approach to the use of artificial intelligence. Integrating these three components –cognitive development, critical thinking, and technological ethics—is indispensable for guiding the application of generative artificial intelligence toward pedagogical and humanistic ends that strengthen cognitive competencies, autonomy, and the reflective capacity of human beings in the twenty-first century.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can produce chemistry lesson plans containing objectives, activities, resources, and assessments, but evaluating their educational contribution requires different kinds of evidence. This critical narrative review examines GenAI-assisted planning for secondary chemistry through three objects of evaluation: the written plan, teachers' professional reasoning and revisions, and students' learning. Seven recent chemistry and science education studies provide the principal contemporary evidence, interpreted alongside research on pedagogical content knowledge, chemical representations, and constructive alignment. The synthesis identifies useful planning support while showing why completed templates, teacher perceptions, and classroom outcomes require separate interpretation. Chemistry-specific review should examine the conditions attached to scientific claims, the connections among representations, the reasoning elicited by tasks, and the responses that trigger instructional adjustment. A worked illustration using electrolysis of aqueous copper sulfate demonstrates how these criteria translate into changes to objectives, diagnostic questions, and follow-up teaching decisions. The article proposes a planning-review procedure and a teacher-education assignment that make justified revisions visible through planning records and discussion. Future studies can connect these records with classroom enactment and student explanations while separating AI assistance from additional opportunities to revise. The review positions teachers' transformation of generated materials as the link between the availability of planning support and the quality of the learning opportunities eventually offered to students.

Foundation models now serve as reasoning layers for robot teams, but it remains unclear whether embodiment-specialized vision-language models (VLMs) preserve the social-reasoning capabilities of general-purpose VLMs. We evaluate Gemini Robotics-ER on SHREC, a benchmark of real human-robot social interactions, and compare it with published general-purpose VLM baselines. Robotics-ER outperforms GPT-4o-mini on error/competence detection but performs worse on detailed social-attribute judgments; adding a visual frame helps one task while hurting the other. These results suggest embodiment-specialized models may perform differently on social judgments that can be read more directly from observable interaction cues versus those requiring more inference about a person's internal state. Because the comparison spans model families, these differences cannot be attributed to embodiment specialization alone. This matters for multi-robot systems, where a shared foundation model could cause systematic social-perception errors to influence multiple coordination decisions. This work presents an initial evaluation, with broader cross-context and video-based analyses left for future work.

Generative artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping higher education, yet potential risks accompany over-reliance on these tools. Grounded in Rogers’ diffusion-of-innovations theory, the present study employed a mixed-methods design. Four waves of independent cross-sectional quantitative data (T1–T4, N = 788) were complemented by semi-structured interviews with 20 undergraduate students. Key patterns emerged as follows: (i) Across later waves, the direct association between external regulation and intrinsic motivation attenuated, while the indirect association operating via identified regulation strengthened. The path from identified regulation to intrinsic motivation was the only relationship that demonstrated significant cross-pair differences while satisfying invariance requirements for all three wave-pair comparisons. Because scalar invariance could not be established, this pattern is interpreted solely as a descriptive group-level temporal trend and should not be read as evidence of intra-individual change. (ii) AI-assisted creativity showed the largest and most consistent downward shift: estimates in later waves were significantly lower relative to the T1 baseline, with effect sizes increasing progressively (Δ = −0.391 to −0.549; d = −0.61 to −0.95; all p < 0.001 following Holm correction). This pattern remained largely unchanged after adjusting for gender, year of study, and academic major, and held up in four predefined subsamples as well as under propensity-score weighting. (iii) The linkage between AI dependency and creativity was significantly positive only at T3 and became negative but non-significant at T4, pointing to a conditional, wave-specific association rather than a stable linear relationship. (iv) Observed wave-level differences for AI dependency and intrinsic motivation did not withstand correction for multiple comparisons. Sensitivity tests yielded only two significant coefficients for AI dependency and none for intrinsic motivation; accordingly, these fluctuations are not given substantive theoretical interpretation. Retrospective qualitative accounts provided supplementary process-oriented context: participants reported initial exposure to AI driven by prevailing social trends, sustained use based on perceived utility, subsequent disappointment in unreliable or misleading outputs, and eventual shifts toward more strategic, self-regulated engagement. Given their retrospective nature, interview narratives were not used to triangulate or validate the quantitative findings. Collectively, this work suggests that as AI-supported learning becomes normalized within a diffusion-driven context, group-level indicators of students’ subjective creative experiences tend to decline. Higher-education institutions may therefore prioritize protecting learners’ creative agency as an explicit educational goal.

Computer-use agents are limited by the interfaces humans give them. An agent may type a spreadsheet cell by cell when a single line of code would do, or print all two thousand lines of a file through a shell to find one function. Both the interfaces and the knowledge of when to use each are built by hand, which cannot keep pace with new applications, workflows, and models. We argue that interface design should itself be an agent capability. We introduce Agent S4, an autonomous computer-use scientist that builds Evolving Agent Interfaces from task experience. A meta-agent examines task agents' trajectories on synthetic training tasks, without success labels, and constructs and revises interfaces and usage knowledge in a repository. Population-based evolution then selects which repositories to develop further by their performance on validation tasks the meta-agent never sees, favoring changes that generalize beyond the seen tasks. On OSWorld V2, Agent S4, with Qwen3.8-27B and the evolved repository of interfaces, sets a new state of the art in open-source computer-use agents, reaching 21.3% binary score, 3.8 times the same model with fixed interfaces. This is above both GPT-5.5 (13.0%) and Claude Opus 4.8 (20.6%), at about 4.3% and 1.5% of their respective costs. On ScienceBoard, the evolved interfaces improve the success rate from 41.4% to 58.6% with the same model. These results suggest that useful interfaces can be evolved from experience, making autonomous interface design a source of improvement complementary to advances in models and harnesses. We open-source our code at https://github.com/simular-ai/agent-s.

Medical AI is often validated under an additive assumption that algorithmic sensitivity and clinician oversight will combine to improve care. We tested this assumption in the high-stakes diagnosis of neonatal pneumoperitoneum, a time-critical surgical emergency. In a multi-reader crossover study analyzing 1750 interpretation events, clinicians reviewed radiographs aided by either a high-reliability model or a systematically error-injected model. We found that high AI reliability paradoxically induces automation bias in trainees, who accepted 52.0% of incorrect suggestions, while offering limited gains to experts. Conversely, when challenged by flawed AI, the three participating neonatologists exhibited a “sentinel behavior” phenotype, correctly overriding 91.7% of errors (Wilson 95% CI: 83.0–96.0%) consistent with increased deliberation; given the small specialist cohort, this finding is hypothesis-generating and warrants prospective replication. We operationalize systemic resilience as the capacity to maintain diagnostic integrity under algorithmic failure and demonstrate that clinical validity depends on the human–AI team’s adversarial resilience rather than standalone accuracy. To mitigate the risk of deskilling and never-skilling, we release an open-source educational sandbox designed to inoculate clinicians against automated errors.

documents.abstract: Industrial maintenance generates near miss narratives that may reveal weaknesses in energy isolation, equipment integrity, permit coordination and other safety barriers. However, interpreting these reports requires contextual judgement, and an automated summary can conceal missing evidence or produce unjustified conclusions. This conceptual paper proposes an evidence-linked artificial intelligence framework for identifying reported barrier degradation and supporting accountable human review. The framework combines a controlled barrier taxonomy, source-linked extraction, retrieval from approved site documents, uncertainty handling and verification of corrective actions. Its central research proposition is that the value of AI should be evaluated through the quality of barrier decisions and the completeness of supporting evidence, rather than classification accuracy alone. A staged mixed methods protocol is specified, including expert annotation, temporal and site-separated testing, comparison with simpler methods, a randomised reviewer study and a prospective shadow deployment. Primary outcomes concern detection of expert-adjudicated barrier concerns, unsupported assertions and reviewer decision quality. Incident reduction is reserved for later investigation and is not inferred from report processing performance. No field dataset, implemented prototype or empirical results are presented. The contribution is a testable research design that connects explainable AI with practical safety assurance while retaining operational authority with competent personnel

Autonomous Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) are in-creasingly being considered for critical applications such as healthcare, finance, cybersecurity, and autonomous transporta-tion. These systems consist of multiple intelligent agents that can independently perceive information, reason about their environment, communicate with other agents, and execute deci-sions. Although multi-agent architectures provide flexibility and scalability, their distributed decision-making process can make the overall system difficult to understand, audit, and verify. Existing Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques such as Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) primarily fo-cus on explaining individual machine-learning predictions. They provide limited support for representing collaborative reasoning, inter-agent communication, conflicts, and collective decisions. This paper proposes an Explainable Decision Graph (EDG) framework for representing the reasoning process of autonomous multi-agent systems in a structured and interpretable form. The proposed framework models agents, observations, evi-dence, communications, intermediate decisions, conflicts, verifi-cation events, and final actions as interconnected graph com-ponents. A verification layer enables decision pathways to be examined against predefined safety and policy constraints. The resulting graph can provide different levels of explanations for end users, developers, and auditors. The paper defines an experimental methodology using multi-agent execution traces and proposes evaluation through ex-planation fidelity, completeness, decision traceability, human comprehensibility, decision accuracy, explanation consistency, and computational overhead. Empirical numerical results are intentionally reserved for the implementation and evaluation stage.

documents.abstract: This study examines the mediating role of financial self-efficacy in the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and the perceived effectiveness of detecting money laundering and financial fraud in Jordanian Islamic banks. The study addresses a behavioral and institutional gap in the literature by explaining how AI-supported monitoring capabilities may be translated into effective regulatory action through employees’ confidence in interpreting and using AI-generated outputs. A quantitative cross-sectional survey design was adopted. Data were collected from 115 employees working in compliance, Shariah compliance, Shariah supervision, internal audit, auditing, and risk management functions in Jordanian Islamic banks. The questionnaire consisted of 35 items measuring AI adoption, financial self-efficacy, perceived AML/fraud detection effectiveness, and demographic characteristics. The data were analyzed using reliability and validity tests, correlation analysis, standardized multiple regression, and regression-based mediation analysis. The results indicate that AI adoption has a statistically significant positive direct effect on perceived AML/fraud detection effectiveness after accounting for financial self-efficacy (β = 0.296, p = 0.001). AI adoption also has a significant positive effect on financial self-efficacy ( β = 0.640, p < 0.001), while financial self-efficacy has a significant positive effect on perceived AML/fraud detection effectiveness ( β = 0.491, p < 0.001). The mediation analysis shows a significant indirect effect of AI adoption on perceived detection effectiveness through financial self-efficacy (indirect effect = 0.314, Sobel z = 4.806, p < 0.001). The VAF value of 51.46% indicates complementary partial mediation. The findings suggest that AI adoption contributes to perceived AML/fraud detection effectiveness not only through technological capabilities but also through employees’ financial self-efficacy. The study recommends integrating AI-supported monitoring systems with structured training, human-in-the-loop governance, and Shariah-sensitive regulatory procedures in Islamic banks.

Abstract There remains much more to Artificial Intelligence than understanding how to learn with neural networks. Inspired in part by how babies, and humans in general, tend to choose for themselves what (and when ) to learn in addition to how to learn, this article discusses similar opportunities, in the areas of multiagent systems and robotics. Grounded in past research on the topic, it categorizes opportunities for choosing what to learn as coming from task decomposition or simplification for difficult problems and/or large environments; unsupervised pre‐training of representations and priors; multiagent learning; and learning from human interaction. The article is based closely on a keynote talk with the same title, delivered at the AAAI‐2026 conference in Singapore on January 22nd, 2026.

Background The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) has raised concerns regarding the authenticity and trustworthiness of synthetic media. Although AI disclosure labels are increasingly used as transparency mechanisms, the cognitive processes through which these cues influence trust formation remain unclear. Objective This study aimed to develop and test a cognitive pathway model explaining how AI disclosure labels, authenticity judgments, perceived risk, cognitive processing styles, and literacy factors shape trust toward AI-generated videos. Methods A 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment was conducted with 617 participants randomly assigned to four conditions involving AI-generated instructional videos with different AI label and video quality combinations. Participants evaluated authenticity, systematic and heuristic processing, trust, perceived risk, adoption intention, sharing intention, AI literacy, and media literacy. Regression, bootstrapped mediation, and moderation analyses were performed. Results AI disclosure labels significantly reduced perceived authenticity but did not directly affect trust, adoption, sharing intention, or perceived risk. Trust formation occurred through cognitive pathways: systematic processing increased trust, whereas heuristic processing reduced trust. Authenticity enhanced trust and lowered perceived risk, with perceived risk mediating the authenticity–trust relationship. Trust positively predicted adoption and sharing intentions, while AI and media literacy moderated selected relationships. Conclusion Trust in AI-generated videos was not directly determined by transparency labels alone. Instead, the observed associations among authenticity judgments, perceived risk, information processing, and trust were consistent with a multi-stage cognitive interpretation, although the cross-sectional post-exposure measurement of these constructs does not establish their temporal or causal sequence.
